bio.en: Max Schoenig is Head of Product at Notion, and has been a PM at Google, ran design at Heroku, and was an engineering and design leader at GitHub.
bio.zh: 马克斯·舍宁（Max Schoenig）是 Notion 的产品负责人，曾在 Google 任 PM、在 Heroku 领导设计，并在 GitHub 担任工程与设计领导。

summary.en: Max argues that in the AI era, skill gaps matter less than agency - the belief that you can change things. He notes the first 10% of every project is now nearly free, lowering the cost of starting. The episode explores how taste and agency, not just technical skill, define modern builders.
summary.zh: 马克斯认为，在 AI 时代，技能差距的重要性低于"自驱力"——即相信自己能改变事物。他指出，如今每个项目的前 10% 几乎免费，降低了启动成本。本期探讨了在现代构建者身上，真正定义价值的为何是品味与自驱力，而非单纯的技术技能。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Before, it was very easy to always say, "Well, I will never be able to do this because insert skill issue." We're realizing that even if you have the skills at your fingertips, the thing that matters is agency. I don't think agency is very evenly distributed in the world.
turns.zh: 以前，我们总是轻易地说"好吧，我永远也做不到这件事，因为存在某个技能上的问题"。但如今我们意识到，即便你掌握了各种技能，真正重要的还是自主行动能力。我认为这种能力在世界上分布得并不均匀。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a piece of advice for someone that wants to develop this within themselves?
turns.zh: 对于那些想要培养这种能力的人，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I tell this to myself, "Hey, do you drive notion like it's stolen?" One day you wake up and you realize the world is made up by people no smarter than you. It just really awakens you to the idea that you can't just change things.
turns.zh: 我对自己说:"嘿，你是不是把Notion当成偷来的工具了？"有一天你醒来，突然意识到这个世界是由和你一样聪明的人组成的。这真的会让你清醒地认识到，你无法轻易改变现状。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you think about your job a couple years ago, what's most changed?
turns.zh: 如果你回想几年前的工作，现在最大的变化是什么？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: The first 10% of every project are now free. It takes almost no effort to now build the first version of a startup.
turns.zh: 现在每个项目的前10%阶段都变得免费了。现在开发初创公司的第一个版本几乎不需要什么努力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Taste comes up a lot now.
turns.zh: 现在"品味"这个词被频繁提及。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Taste actually means you're able to run a virtual machine in your head where given an idea, you can predict for a certain in group whether they're going to like it or not. You just have to do reps. It's almost like training a model.
turns.zh: 品味实际上意味着你能够在脑海中运行一个虚拟模拟器。给定一个想法，你就能预测某个群体是否会喜欢它。你只需要不断练习。这几乎就像训练一个模型。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you think matters to building a successful product?
turns.zh: 你认为打造成功产品的关键是什么？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: All the great products have something tiny that is a superpower, one tiny core that is so exceptionally good. One of the biggest pitfalls is if you get into the loop of, if I just add one more thing to the product, it'll be finally great. That never works.
turns.zh: 所有伟大的产品都有一个微小的超级能力，一个极其出色的核心部分。最大的陷阱之一是如果你陷入这样的循环:只要我再给产品添加一个功能，它就会变得非常棒。但这永远行不通。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Give this hot take on universal basic income.
turns.zh: 谈谈你对全民基本收入的看法吧。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: We already have universal basic income. It's called knowledge work.
turns.zh: 我们已经有了全民基本收入。它叫做知识工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Today, my guest is Max Max Schoening. Max is a hard person to describe. He was a product manager at Google. He ran the design team at Heroku. He was a design leader and an engineer at GitHub under Nat Friedman. He's also a two-time founder and is now head of product at Notion. He's one of the most successful AI forward product leaders out there. And as you'll soon see, one of the deepest thinkers on how AI impacts how we build and how we use software. (00:01:41): Before we get into it, don't forget to check out lennysproductpass.com for an insane set of deals available exclusively to Lenny's newsletter subscribers. With that, I bring you Max Schoening. (00:01:55): Max, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 今天的嘉宾是Max Schoening。Max是一个很难描述的人。他曾是谷歌的产品经理，负责Heroku的设计团队，还在Nat Friedman手下担任GitHub的设计负责人和工程师。他两次创业，现在是Notion的产品负责人。他是AI前沿产品领导者中最成功的之一，正如你很快就会发现的，他也是对AI如何影响我们构建和使用软件最有深刻见解的人之一。(00:01:41): 在我们开始之前，别忘了访问l越来越多的交易仅对Lenny's新闻通讯订阅者开放。接下来，我为您介绍Max Schoening。(00:01:55): Max，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Thank you for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢邀请。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I am so excited to have you here. I feel like there's this quote I think about when I think about you and you being on this podcast. It comes from the Bible. And just paraphrasing, the quote is, "I was made for such a time as this." (00:02:12): I feel like there's all this talk about roles merging, designers becoming PMs, engineers, everyone's the same, the Venn diagrams collapsing. You've been that for a long time. It's hard to even describe what you are and what you've done. You've done all the things. So I feel like you have such a unique insight into where things are heading. (00:02:28): I want to start with just this broad question. What have you seen about where things are going for product teams for product building as AI becomes more powerful, as we integrate it more into our workflows? And I ask you this because I've heard from so many people at Notion that you are the reason that designers are shipping code, PMs are shipping code. You're not just living in the future, you're pushing the whole team and company to live in the future. (00:02:52): And so coming back to the question, just like, what are you seeing about where things are going? What will change? What will people realize in the next few months, years that you're already seeing?
turns.zh:
很高兴你能来参加这次访谈。每当想到你和你的团队参与这个播客时，我总会想起一句圣经中的名言：“我被造就，是为了成就这个时代。” （00:02:12）我觉得现在人们总在谈论角色融合、设计师转做产品经理、工程师职责模糊、Venn图重叠等话题。但你早就是这样的存在了。你所做的一切都太难用言语形容了。你几乎参与了所有领域，所以我相信你对未来趋势有着独特的洞察力。

（00:02:28）首先我想抛出一个宏观问题：随着人工智能变得更加强大，且我们将其深度融入工作流程，产品团队和产品开发会走向何方？我之所以这么问，是因为Notion公司的许多人都说，你是设计师写代码、产品经理写代码的幕后推手。你不只是预见未来，而是推动整个团队和公司去拥抱未来。

（00:02:52）回到核心问题：你对未来的趋势有何观察？哪些变化即将发生？未来几个月或几年内，人们会意识到哪些你早已洞察的趋势？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Well, first of all, when you said a quote from the Bible, I was very curious where this was going to head.
turns.zh: 首先，当你提到圣经引语时，我很好奇接下来会怎么发展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's the first time I've quoted the Bible on this podcast, I think.
turns.zh: 这应该是我在播客中首次引用圣经经文吧。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I wouldn't take credit for the designers at Notion and the PMs at Notion now code. I think that would have probably happened anyways, but I can tell you the origin story of it, which is when I joined Notion, we were building a lot of chat interfaces and we were designing the chat interfaces in Figma. And there's this great talk by Bret Victor, Stop Drawing Dead Fish, which essentially is ... I mean, the static image of a chat is basically the dead fish here. (00:03:45): You have to feel the AI to some degree. And so two designers, myself, just put together the worst possible playground you could think of of a small code base that is very LLM-friendly, used the tools that LLMs are very good at using. And then we moved all of our prototyping for specifically the chat interfaces to that.
turns.zh:
我不会把Notion的设计师和产品经理现在写代码这件事归功于自己。我觉得这无论如何都会发生，但我可以讲讲背后的故事。当我加入Notion时，我们正在开发大量聊天界面，并在Figma中进行设计。布雷特·维克多（Bret Victor）有一场精彩的演讲《别再画死鱼了》，基本上就是说……我是指，静态的聊天界面就像那条死鱼。
（00:03:45）你必须在某种程度上感知到AI的存在。所以两位设计师和我拼凑了一个可能最糟糕的代码实验场，专门针对LLM友好的小代码库，使用LLM擅长的工具。然后，我们把所有聊天界面的原型都迁移到了这个平台上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And just to understand this playground concept, essentially, this is an idea of people work within this separate area with AI tools versus their whole Notion code base, making it really easy to get started and try stuff.
turns.zh: 要理解这个实验场的概念，本质上就是让人们在一个与AI工具隔离的区域内工作，与整个Notion代码库分开，这样既能轻松上手尝试新东西。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Yes. And that was the first version. It aligned with model capabilities at the time. We don't always use ... maybe at Notion, the main code base is not always the most agent-friendly because iterations and a decade of patterns. And so we optimized for, okay, how can we make this the least scary and most one-shottable so that people would just have to overcome this oh, the fear of the terminal, but then it just becomes chatting. And we recreated a bunch of the patterns and UIs that exist in that playground. (00:04:55): Now, the good news is that's just to get people on the treadmill because as model capabilities get better, now we have the same designers and PMs also just contributing to the production code base to a lesser degree, of course. But like you can see where the trend is headed as model capabilities get better. The amount of work that you can do is obviously going to increase exponentially.
turns.zh: 是的。那是第一个版本。它与当时的模型能力相契合。我们并非总是使用……比如在Notion，主代码库并不总是最适合代理的，因为经过十年的迭代和模式形成。我们优化后的目标是，如何让这项技术尽可能不令人恐惧且一次性可用，让人们只需克服对终端的恐惧，然后它就变成了一种聊天体验。我们重新创建了在那个平台上存在的许多模式和用户界面。（00:04:55）：现在，好消息是，这只是为了让人们开始接触这项技术，因为随着模型能力的提升，现在同样的设计师和产品经理也只是在较小程度上为生产代码库做出贡献。当然，但正如你所看到的，随着模型能力的提升，趋势正在朝着这个方向发展。你能完成的工作量显然会呈指数级增长。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I feel so uncomfortable predicting the future in terms of where things are heading because, well, predicting exponentials is really hard, but I'll take the stab at, it is very, very useful for designers to move from manipulating Figma documents into code. That has always been useful. I've always been camp designers should code. In a previous life, I led design and product at GitHub and GitHub designers before LLMs contributed to GitHub, I think and the top contributors to GitHub itself, like 10% were designers. (00:07:19): Right now, processes are breaking. One is we have designers who now mostly code and prototype in code, and then they are asked by other teams in marketing and so on to reverse engineer that in Figma because they use that to create assets for videos and so on. And so obviously, that is kind of silly. That seems like busy work. (00:07:42): On the pushing to production, I think it's a spectrum, obviously small changes, styling tweaks and so on. It's a given that you can just do that now. I do have a general maybe issue with vibe coding in the sense of I don't feel like the quality of software has increased all that much in the last 12 months. I think maybe the amount of software has, but it's very, very hard to find software that is reliable. And so the way we see it is it's not so much about pushing to production and having designers deploy. It's about them thinking and designing in the medium that will actually end up being the real thing once engineering takes it over.
turns.zh:
预测未来的发展方向实在太难了，尤其是指数级增长的趋势。但我还是要大胆说一句：对于设计师来说，从在Figma中操作到写代码的转变，实在太有意义了。这一转变一直以来都很有价值。我一直主张设计师应该具备编程能力。在GitHub的早期（在大模型兴起之前），设计师和产品经理是推动GitHub发展的主力军，当时GitHub的顶级贡献者中，约有10%是设计师。（00:07:19）：但当下流程正在崩坏。比如，有些设计师现在主要用代码进行原型设计，然后又被其他团队（比如市场部）要求把这些代码反向转换成Figma文件，用于制作视频素材。这显然很不明智，简直是无用功。  
（00:07:42）：再说上线流程，显然这是一个连续体。小改动、样式调整之类的，现在都可以直接上线。这没问题。但我对用代码写代码的趋势有些担忧。过去12个月里，软件质量似乎没有显著提升，产出量倒是增加了，但可靠的软件却越来越难找。所以关键不在于设计师必须上线代码，而在于他们要学会用最终的技术媒介进行思考和设计，这样工程团队接手后才能顺畅推进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's all this talk about designers should be shipping code, PM should be shipping code. And then there's the flip side of, because engineers can move so fast, there's so much more happening, things are moving all the time. Designers and PMs are squeezed more and more because it's hard to stand top of all these things that are constantly shipping. And so maybe it doesn't actually make sense for designers and PMs to be spending time coding. And instead, their time is better spent making sure things are moving in a direction that makes sense for the business. It's cohesive. What's your thoughts on just that balance?
turns.zh: 现在大家都在说设计师应该写代码，产品经理应该写代码。但反过来，由于工程师开发速度太快，新功能层出不穷，设计师和产品经理的压力也越来越大，因为要时刻跟上这些快速上线的项目。或许设计师和产品经理花时间写代码并不明智，他们的时间更应该用来确保项目方向符合业务需求，保持连贯性。对此你们怎么看？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I actually don't care at all whether designers write code that lands in production. The reason I like thinking in code is because it forces you to consider the medium. If then all of that gets thrown out, great. So, for example, I think the two extremes would be if a PM or a designer knows how to tweak with, pick your favorite, they're all the same, Codex, Claude Code or whatever. If they know how to tweak small details of the UI, but they don't understand how an agent loop works, I would much rather take the designer or PM that deeply has an affinity for understanding how agent loops work and can design those than someone who can write traditional software and tweak styles. (00:09:41): And that's really hard because I think the only way that you can actually get to understanding agent loops is if you build them in the material that they're made of, which is currently code. And increasingly so if you look at all the coding harnesses, basically, the operating systems of the '90s. And so, I think that's why I care that people code, not because of the utility of shipping to production, but because it forces you to really interrogate the material that you're designing with.
turns.zh: 其实我根本不在乎设计师写的代码是否能上线。我喜欢用代码思考的原因是它能迫使你审视媒介本身。如果所有这些思考都被抛弃，那也很好。但举个例子，两个极端情况：如果产品经理或设计师只会调整用户界面的小细节，却不理解代理循环的工作原理，我宁愿选择深深理解代理循环并能设计它们的设计师或产品经理，而不是只会写传统软件和调整样式的人。（00:09:41）：这很难，因为真正理解代理循环的唯一方法，就是用它们所依赖的媒介——当前就是代码来构建它们。特别是当你看看所有编程框架时，它们基本上就是90年代的操作系统。所以我才希望人们学习编程，不是因为上线的好处，而是因为这能迫使你真正审视你所设计的媒介。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it's more the prototyping use cases than we're just going to be shipping more features because we can.
turns.zh: 因此，更多的是原型设计用例，而不是我们只是因为能做到就想上线更多功能。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: It tends to be that once you awaken someone to a new material, that at some point they also blur the lines and then write production code. But I think it's really important not to forget that the reason why is to become a master of the material, not a cog in the delivery mechanism for the idea.
turns.zh: 通常，一旦你让某人意识到一种新材料的可能性，他们往往会模糊界限，进而编写生产代码。但我认为重要的是，不要忘记这样做的原因是为了精通该领域，而不是成为某个创意交付机制中的齿轮。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really interesting. What do you find is key to people being successful in this new world? There's a lot of designers, a lot of PMs at Notion. What do you find is separating the ones that are thriving and will do well in this coming future versus ones that may fall behind?
turns.zh: 这真的很有趣。在你看来，人们要在新世界中取得成功的关键是什么？Notion有很多设计师和产品经理。你认为哪些人能在未来蓬勃发展，而哪些人可能会落后？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I suspect that this is also something that has always been the case, and we would just categorize this as founder versus not. And do you start a startup versus not, which is agency. I think before, it was very easy to always say, "Well, I will never be able to do this because insert skill issue." And I think we're realizing that even if you have the skills at your fingertips because now, I don't know, an AGI adjacent model helps you. The thing that matters is agency, and I don't think agency is very evenly distributed in the world. (00:11:27): And I think people who have true agency and they understand that the world around them is malleable will do great. And the folks who stick to, "Tell me really, what does it mean to be a PM? What does it mean to be a designer? And what's my job as an engineer?" I think that will be much harder and cultivate agency. I think that's the thing.
turns.zh: 我怀疑这其实一直都是如此，我们只需将其归类为创业者与非创业者之分。是创办初创公司，还是不创办初创公司——这就是区别所在。过去，人们总是很容易说：“好吧，我永远做不到这件事，因为存在技能缺失的问题。”但现在我们意识到，即便你掌握了技能，因为比如说通用人工智能相关模型能助你一臂之力。关键在于自主行动力，而这种能力在世界上分布并不均匀。（00:11:27）：我认为真正具有自主行动力的人，他们明白周围的世界是可塑的，将会大放异彩。而那些执着于“告诉我，到底什么是产品经理？什么是设计师？我作为工程师的职责是什么？” 的人，我认为他们会遇到更多困难，难以培养出自主行动力。这才是关键所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of someone using agency ... a good example at Notion of someone just leaning into that and doing ... and maybe shipping something, changing the way something was happening at Notion, just to give us a like, "Oh, wow. I see what you're talking about"?
turns.zh: 有没有人利用自主行动力的例子……在Notion，有没有人能真正发挥这种能力，做出一些事情，比如改变Notion的运作方式，让我们感叹“哇，原来你说的是这个意思”？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Notinos are, this was surprising to me, especially on the design team way above average agency compared to other places that I've worked at.
turns.zh: 让我惊讶的是，Notion的员工，尤其是设计团队的自主行动力水平，远超我在其他公司工作时见过的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And Notinos, by the way, are Notion employees.
turns.zh: 对了，顺便说一下，Notion员工就是指Notion的员工。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Yes, sorry.
turns.zh: 是的，抱歉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: [inaudible 00:12:17]. I would say one example would be someone like Brian Levin, who you should probably have on the podcast at some point.
turns.zh: [00:12:17不可听清]。我想举一个例子，比如Brian Levin，你应该找个机会邀请他上播客。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He was on our sister podcast, How I AI. We'll link to that episode.
turns.zh: 他上过我们的姐妹播客《How I AI》。我们会附上那期节目的链接。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: There we go. Yeah. You should cut this one short and have him on. I think the way I would describe it is, and I tell this to myself as well, which is like, okay, do you drive Notion like it's stolen, which is we're not the founders. We're coming in after there was already insane product market fit, but you can still contribute to the company in a way that you feel agency and you're not just like, it's what's your role? And so Brian obviously already blurs engineering and design, but he also is probably our number one recruiter in terms of, "Hey, this is what the org needs. I'm going to go out and talk to people and find someone." (00:13:05): And I think that is a thing that just demonstrates it's out of the day-to-day and it demonstrates the, "No, I want to just affect change. I don't care how it happens." Eric Lou is another one, the fact that he went from writing a lot of strategy docs to, he asked me at some point, he's like, "Hey, look, at some point in the future, if you started a startup, would you hire me?" And I said, "Well, not in the first 10. I don't need a product manager." And he's like, "Oh, okay. I'm going to work on the skills so that you would hire me in the first five." (00:13:34): And that led to first spending more time in Figma instead of writing long PRDs. And now it's just, why do I have to do the Figma thing? Can't I just build the prototype and at least show you what I think and do the thinking in there? And so those are just sort of signs of high agency of I'm going to change the role to how I think it should be.
turns.zh: 好了。是的。你应该把这段剪短点，直接请他上台。我觉得我会这么形容这件事——我也常这样告诫自己——就是，别把Notion当作自己偷来的，毕竟我们不是创始人。我们加入时，产品市场匹配度已经极高，但你仍然能以一种有自主感的方式为公司做出贡献，而不只是被动接受角色定位。比如布莱恩显然就把工程和设计融合在了一起，但他同时还是我们头号招聘高手。他会说，“组织需要这个人才，我去找人吧。”（00:13:05）我觉得这恰恰说明他跳出了日常框架，展现出“不，我要推动变革，过程如何并不重要”的决心。埃里克·卢也是个例子。他从大量撰写战略文档，转变为主动提问：“未来如果你创办公司，会不会雇佣我？”我回答：“前十年不会，我不需要产品经理。”他回应：“那好，我要提升技能，让你前五年就录用我。”（00:13:34）这促使他从撰写冗长的PRD文档转向花更多时间在Figma上设计原型。现在他总在问：“为什么非要用Figma？能不能直接构建原型，至少让我展示思路然后再润色？” 这些都是自主权增强的典型表现——他们在重塑理想中的工程师角色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something you mentioned earlier, which I love, this idea of just rethinking what is this role of engineering, what should it be if we didn't have this meme already for it? I wonder what we lose as these roles start to merge. We used to have this clear engineer, product manager, designer. And as people start to ... as you talk about malleable software, we'll come back to this, but like malleable roles almost, there's something we lose like clear career paths and design consistency, things like that.
turns.zh: 你之前提到的观点很棒，就是重新思考工程师的角色定位。如果没有现成的刻板印象，工程师该是什么样的？我很好奇角色融合会带来哪些损失。过去有明确的工程师、产品经理、设计师角色，但随着软件可塑性增强，角色边界逐渐模糊。我们会回归这个话题，但这几乎意味着失去清晰的职业路径和设计一致性等核心要素。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I think if we're not careful, we will lose specialists. And so the way I would describe this is, I sometimes like to think about software in terms of physical metaphors, right? And physical metaphors somehow make it so much clearer what a prototype is versus what an engineered thing is. And if you and I were to build a hardware startup, well, we would make the first enclosures and prototypes with 3D printing and you would see all the layer lines, it would be very, very obvious to you that this is not a thing that you should just give to people to pay for. (00:14:55): And then there's a long, windy road all the way to the end where at some point, if you're very lucky, you get to manufacture that product for, I don't know, 100 million people. And so then the engineering is actually the, how do I optimize the factory so that we have enough yield and so that we have enough precision? (00:15:13): And that to me, I think, is very absent right now from most of the discourse in software, which is it's all about how many tokens can we spend and how many features can we ship? And I'm like, okay, but where's the engineering part? And the engineering part is the, you make sure that this thing works for a hundred million people, for a billion people. (00:15:31): And on the design side, I think there is the, yes, anyone can now very quickly take a design system off the shelf, build a very usable user interface, get to the core of what's really important, but where's the delight in craft? And so I think we have to make sure that we, in this sort of merging of roles, don't lose the specialists on the edges. And yeah, I would say that's something would potentially be sad if we lost it.
turns.zh: 我认为如果我们不加注意，我们会失去专业人才。说到这里，我有时喜欢用物理类比来理解软件，正确吗？物理类比能让人们更清楚地理解原型和工程化产品的区别。假如你和我要创办一家硬件初创公司，我们会用3D打印制作首批外壳和原型，你会看到所有的层线，这会让你很清楚，这可不是能随便拿去卖钱的东西。（00:14:55）：然后是漫长而曲折的道路，最终如果你运气好，也许能为1亿人生产产品。接下来，工程环节的核心在于如何优化工厂产能，确保良品率和精度达标？（00:15:13）：在我看来，这在当下软件行业的讨论中基本缺失了。大家只谈论能花多少代币、能上线多少功能。我会问，工程环节在哪里？工程环节就是要确保产品能服务1亿甚至10亿用户。（00:15:31）：在设计层面，我认为虽然现在任何人都能快速套用现成的设计系统，打造易用的用户界面，直击核心需求，但精心打磨的乐趣哪去了？所以在角色融合的过程中，我们要确保边缘领域的专业人才不被边缘化。如果失去这些人才，确实会令人遗憾。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to this agency piece because I feel like people hear this word a lot on this podcast. Yes, agency. For someone that wants to build this within themselves or even just understand, do I have agency? I don't know. I think I do. I imagine everyone listening is like, yes, I am huge. I have huge agency. I'm such an agent and I'll do what needs to be done. Do you have a piece of advice for someone that wants to develop this within themselves?
turns.zh: 我想再谈谈“自主性”这个概念，因为在播客里经常听到这个词。是的，自主性。对于那些想在自己身上培养这种能力，或者想判断自己是否有自主性的人，我不知道。我觉得自己有自主性。想象听众会说，没错，我超有自主性。我就是个行动派，会把事情做好。对于想培养自主性的人，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Partially the reason why I'm in software is the thing that I care most about is the Steve Jobs quote, "One day you wake up and you realize the world is made up by people no smarter than you." And there are basically people who realize this by themselves or they have an amazing teacher early on in their life that encourages this. And the biggest through line I've found is making. (00:16:49): I think if you tinker and if you make things, then you are now on this treadmill of just creating and then you're like, "Oh, it's actually not that hard to learn how to make that chair in my office or let me tweak it a little bit." Or maybe, I don't know, it's like a home cooked meal is a form of tinkering ironically. And I think the more you can do that in life, I think actually making things is the innately human toolmaking, creating art and so on. (00:17:18): So just do that versus I think when a lot of people hear agency, they think of themselves as they're in this big machine and they're like, "Oh, okay, I'm going to circumvent my terrible boss or manager or whatever so that I get X, Y, and Z." It's like, no, no, just start by making things. And usually, when you get better at making things at some point, people pay attention and it just really awakens you to the idea that you can just change things.
turns.zh:
部分原因在于，我投身软件行业的原因是我最珍视史蒂夫·乔布斯的那句话：“某天你醒来，突然意识到这个世界是由和你一样聪明的人组成的。” 基本上，要么人们自己领悟到这一点，要么在生命早期遇到一位出色的导师来启发他们。而我发现最重要的共通点就是创造。（00:16:49）我认为如果你喜欢鼓捣、喜欢动手制作东西，那么你就会踏上不断创造的旅程。比如，“哦，学会如何制作办公室里的那把椅子其实没那么难”，或者“让我稍微调整一下它”。又或者，可能吧，不知为何，讽刺的是，一顿家常菜也是一种动手创造。我认为在生活中越多地实践创造，越能感受到创造的乐趣——这本质上就是人类与生俱来的工具制造天性，是艺术创作等等。
（00:17:18）所以就去做吧。我觉得很多人听到“主动性”这个词时，会把自己想象成身处巨大机器中的人，然后想：“好吧，我要绕过糟糕的老板或经理之类的，这样就能得到X、Y和Z了。” 但不不不，先从动手创造开始。通常，当你越来越擅长创造时，人们会注意到你，这会让你意识到你可以改变现状。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this. There's this meme on Twitter, you could just do things. I love this version of it. You could just change things, which is a good segue to something you've been a big, I don't know, advocate of and proponent of this idea of malleable software, something you mentioned earlier. It feels like something that wasn't actually possible and now is like, okay, I could see exactly what you're talking about now. You've been honest from before the AI revolution. (00:18:10): Talk about just this idea, malleable software, why you think it's so important, what you think people need to be thinking about here.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个观点。推特上有个梗，叫“你可以直接行动”。我喜欢这种版本。你可以直接改变现状，这和您一直大力倡导的可塑性软件理念很契合。您之前就提到过这个概念。感觉这在过去根本不可行，但现在却变得现实了。现在我完全明白您的意思了。您在人工智能革命之前就对此坦诚了。（00:18:10）能否谈谈可塑性软件这个概念？为什么您认为它如此重要？您认为人们在这一领域需要关注什么？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Malleable software is the idea that software works closer to the interest of the people that use it than the interest of the corporation that makes it, maybe that's how I'd frame it. And in particular, I don't want to use software that is specifically just designed by the ivory tower in Cupertino. And I say this as a huge Apple fanboy, but imagine you lived in an environment where you do not get to rearrange your living room and the kitchen has to be exactly set up the way that someone else decided. We would not take that, right? But that is kind of the world that we have in software right now where we have this world of apps and apps are like this very, every layer is glued together of like the user interface, the data ownership and so on. And it's like this little square on your phone. (00:19:08): And the moment you're like, "Okay, this is a really great app, but I just want to change a little bit." That is usually not possible, the behavior. You have the flip side, which is you could run your own Linux distribution and go that way. And I think then what happens is you realize, "Oh, okay, I like the malleability, but I also have other things to do and I don't always want to start from scratch and figure out why the trackpad doesn't work." And so to me, it just comes back down to, do you have ownership over your computing life? And I think increasingly, we don't. (00:19:42): Now, you brought this up presumably because I think you may have not thought about malleable software too much before AI, but now you're making your own tools maybe for podcast recording, for prepping for shows or, I don't know, whatever. There's a myriad examples and people are awakening to this idea of like, "Oh, I can just make tools." And that is a form of malleable software, but it has to be built on top of a platform or an operating system that encourages this because otherwise, we're just doing individual ... (00:20:15): Everybody has their own individual little tool. And I don't know, I like working with people and I like communal tools. And I don't know, this is a thing that the folks at Ink & Switch are obviously are at the forefront. I get to work with Geoffrey Litt every single day now that spend a lot of time thinking about how would we make software more malleable so that we feel more ownership over it without going back a long time and not having real-time collaboration and the security aspects and so on.
turns.zh:
灵活的软件理念在于，软件应更贴近用户的需求，而非开发公司的利益诉求——或许我可以这样来概括。特别是，我不愿使用那些由苹果园区设计师闭门造车的产品。作为苹果的忠实粉丝，我要说的是：假如你生活在一个环境中，无法随意布置客厅，而厨房布局必须完全遵循他人设定的模式，我们肯定不会接受这种设定。然而，当前软件世界却如同这个被设计成方盒子的手机应用生态：用户界面、数据所有权等每一层都被封闭式地黏合在一起。（00:19:08）当你想稍作调整时，却往往面临无法实现的困境。这就如同你试图自定义 Linux 发行版，却发现要从零开始调试触摸板失灵的问题。归根结底，关键在于你是否能掌控自己的计算生活。如今，越来越多人意识到这一点却无能为力。

（00:19:42）你提到这个话题，或许是因为在人工智能时代之前，你未曾深入思考过灵活软件的概念。但如今你可能在开发播客录制工具、节目准备工具等应用——无数例子表明，人们正逐渐觉醒于“我可以自己动手创造工具”的意识。这本身就是灵活软件的体现，但前提是平台或操作系统必须支持这种理念，否则我们只能各自为战。

（00:20:15）每个人都开发着独立的小工具，但我更倾向于与他人合作，使用共享工具。Ink & Switch 团队在这方面显然走在前沿。我现在每天与 Geoffrey Litt 合作，致力于如何让软件更具灵活性，让我们在不回溯历史、无需实时协作、兼顾安全性等前提下，更强地掌控自己的计算生活。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really love, and I just want to make sure we highlight this idea you're sharing. It's something that I learned also from Brian Chesky at Airbnb, this idea that you can change things, that the things around you are just made by other people that may not actually be smarter than you. And it's just this really empowering thing to always think about that things can change. This isn't the way things have to be forever. Humans made this thing, like humans made this phone and there are better approaches that other humans ... that you can come up with, other people will come up with. (00:21:19): What I think about as I think about this is there's a video that you pinned to your Twitter profile that we'll link to, which I think is Dieter Rams. Is that who the person is? Okay. He's walking around and he's just criticizing all these designed chairs. Talk about what that video's trying to ... Why you pin that to your profile?
turns.zh:
我非常欣赏你分享的这个理念。这也是我从爱彼迎的布莱恩·切斯基那里学到的，即你可以改变现状，身边的事物不过是其他人设计的，他们未必比你更聪明。时刻保持事物可变的思维模式，非常有力量。事情不必永远如此。人类创造了这些东西，比如手机，我们能想到更好的方法，其他人也会想出更好的方案。

（00:21:19）谈到这点时，我想到你推送到推特主页的视频，链接我们会附上，里面是迪特·拉姆斯。他四处评判各种设计椅子。你为什么会把这个视频放在推特主页？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: There's many reasons. One is, I think maybe the only thing that I have in common with this very accomplished person is that we're both German. And so sometimes I joke that I also aspire to disapprovingly just point at things with my walking stick and say, "This isn't good enough. This isn't good enough." (00:21:57): The reason why is because I think if you speak German, this is one of the funniest clips that I've ever ... I just die laughing every single time. I'm actually curious how you think about how it ties to malleable software because the main reason why I use that as a clip of reference is I'm very much in the camp of design should be first useful and then beautiful. And I think a lot of the pieces there are predominantly things that you put in a museum for display. And if you try to sit on them, you'd be like, "What is this nonsense?"
turns.zh: 原因有很多。其中之一是，我觉得我和这位成就卓著的人唯一的共同点就是我们都是德国人。所以有时我开玩笑说，我也渴望用拐杖指着东西不满地说：“这不够好。这不够好。”（00:21:57）之所以这么说，是因为我觉得如果你会德语，这段视频绝对是最搞笑的……每次看都笑得不行。说实话，我很好奇你怎么看待它与可塑性软件的关系，因为我用这段视频作为参考的主要原因是我深信设计应该先实用，再美观。而展览中的许多作品更多的是供人观赏的艺术品。试想你坐在上面会觉得：“这什么破玩意儿？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I felt there is just like you see all ... I would think it was Frank Gehry and all these famous designers' pieces put up in a museum. And I think to most people, it'd be like, "Wow, this is so incredible and beautiful." You see somebody that has a status and a reputation and you assume this is great. And I love that he breaks that veil of like, "No, this is so stupid, what is this? What does this bunch of cabinets tie together? Doesn't make any sense."
turns.zh: 我当时的感觉就是，就像你看到所有……我会以为是弗兰克·盖里和其他知名设计师的作品陈列在博物馆里一样。我觉得对大多数人来说，这会让人惊叹：“哇，这太不可思议了，太美了。” 你看到一个享有盛誉的人物，就会想“哇，这太棒了。” 但我喜欢他打破这种幻觉，比如“不，这太蠢了，这是什么？这堆柜子有什么关联？根本说不通。”

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: For that cabinet, I think he says something like, "It is neither orderly nor properly chaotic." I understand the connection now. The timeless way of building and Stewart Brand's How Buildings Learn, I think, idea is also that it's very likely that the best homes for you are not actually built by an architect. They are the thing that over a long time adapt to exactly how you would love to lead your life and they learn over time versus immediately. (00:23:32): And so then that is obviously a very costly version of malleability if you have to rip out a wall or whatever. But I think the main thing that Dieter Rams points out there is it should be a thing that's useful and a good way to figure out how something is useful is if you can change it and tweak it. Makes sense.
turns.zh: 关于那个柜子，我记得他说了句：“它既不整齐，也不恰当的混乱。” 现在我明白其中的关联了。永恒的建筑方式和斯图尔特·布兰德的《建筑如何学习》的理念也在于，最适合你的家很可能不是由建筑师建造的。而是那些随着时间逐渐适应你生活方式的家居，它们是随着时间而演变的，而不是一蹴而就的。（00:23:32）所以如果你要拆掉一堵墙之类的，那显然是昂贵的可塑性版本。但我认为迪特尔·拉姆斯强调的核心观点是，它应该实用，而判断某物是否实用的最好方法就是能否对其进行改动和调整。这很合理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It all connects. It all connects. Okay.
turns.zh: 一切都联系起来了。一切都联系起来了。好的。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I get it now.
turns.zh: 现在我懂了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There you go. And we'll link to it. It's really funny to watch. I wish I understood the German. (00:24:01): I want to come back to this idea of malleable software from a perspective of SaaS and the SaaS apocalypse. There's all this talk about, we will not need SaaS tools any longer. We will build all our own tools. We don't need Salesforce. Imagine some people are like, "We don't need Notion. I'm going to build my own Notion." You have a hot take there. Talk about what you think is going to happen.
turns.zh: 就是这样。我们会附上链接。看这个视频真的很有趣。真希望我能听懂德语。（00:24:01）我想从SaaS和SaaS末日的角度来探讨可塑性软件这个概念。到处都在说我们不再需要SaaS工具了，我们要自己搭建工具，不需要Salesforce了。想象有人说：“我们不需要Notion，我要自己搭建Notion。”你有什么独到见解吗？谈谈你对未来趋势的看法。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: If you just think about what SaaS ... The problem is the moment you have an acronym, it means a lot of very specific things. And if you're going to say, "Hey, is this type of SaaS that we've built in the 2010s just as relevant as it was in the 2010s?" The answer would be, it would be silly to say, "No, nothing's going to change. It'll be the same." Because I think you can say a lot of SaaS in the 2010s was a very, very fancy form around a spreadsheet or something more generic. And the thing it did is it just guided people in the right direction to fill out that form, as in it is less malleable than a spreadsheet and that is the value. The as a service part is I think the thing that actually matters, which is I don't think most people actually want to maintain the full stack of software. (00:25:09): And so whenever I see someone and I am someone here say, "Oh, I just rebuilt this piece of software." I've tried rebuilding Notion in a weekend for myself just to push at the edges of frustrating things. I don't think people want that. I think, for the most part, it's nice if you can just ... People don't want to go hunting either. They just want to go to Costco and have the steak in a styrofoam packaging and pretend that it wasn't hunting or an animal in the first place. I think with software, Bret Taylor says this too, software is like a garden, you need to tend to it. And the thing you pay for as a service is the maintenance and a bunch of specialists thinking really hard about a problem. (00:25:51): And so I don't think that's going away. What I would probably say is that tools will become more general. I mean, I'm obviously biased. I work at Notion. I like Notion and I consider Notion to be fairly malleable, not enough. I think it should become more malleable. We internally joked, Joanna Stern, a journalist, recently tweeted something along the lines of, "Oh, thanks to Notion AI, I finally understand and use Notion." I don't know what that says about Notion. And to me, this is a great example of Notion wasn't SaaS in the traditional way. It's kind of hard to get started, but because of AI now, people can ... they have a tutor essentially and can build more things. (00:26:32): And so I suspect that software will go more back into the '90s of general tools, WordProcessor, spreadsheet, FileMaker Pro, that kind of thing, but those will still be as a service. And then you'll still have specialized tools around security and so on of just people who go the extra mile to really solve a user problem. So I think to some degree the SaaS apocalypse is greatly exaggerated. At the same time, are things going to stay the same? Of course not. Why would they?
turns.zh: 假如你只考虑 SaaS……问题在于，一旦你有了个缩写术语，它就代表着很多非常具体的含义。假如你要问：“嘿，我们在2010年代开发的这类SaaS，现在是否还和当时一样实用？”答案会是，否认这一点简直太荒谬了。因为我觉得2010年代的很多SaaS不过是电子表格之类更通用工具的华丽包装。它们的价值在于能引导用户正确填写表格，但本质上缺乏灵活性。这才是SaaS真正重要的部分——我认为大多数人其实并不想维护整套软件栈。（00:25:09）每当我看到有人说自己“重建了某个软件”时，我都会翻白眼。我曾试着在一个周末重建Notion，只为突破那些令人沮丧的功能极限。但我觉得人们并不想要这样。他们更倾向于“拿来即用”。就像去Costco超市买块用泡沫包装的牛排，假装自己从未猎杀过动物。Bret Taylor也说过，软件就像花园，需要悉心打理。而SaaS服务的核心价值在于维护和专业团队深度钻研难题。（00:25:51）我认为这种模式不会消失。我更倾向于认为工具会变得更加通用。我在Notion工作，自然对其青睐有加。我认为Notion本应更具灵活性，但目前还不够。我希望它能进一步增强可定制性。我们内部曾开玩笑，记者Joanna Stern最近在推特上写道“多亏了Notion的AI，我终于理解并学会了使用Notion”。这让我对Notion有了更深的认识。在我看来，Notion并非传统意义上的SaaS。它上手难度较高，但借助AI技术，用户如今能获得类似导师的指导，创造更多可能。（00:26:32）我预计软件会回归到90年代的通用工具时代——文字处理器、电子表格、FileMaker Pro之类。但这些工具仍将以SaaS形式存在。同时，专业工具将继续涌现，专注于安全等领域，帮助用户深度解决问题。总之，SaaS末日论被严重夸大了。但事物会保持变化吗？当然会。为什么不呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I completely agree. I think people think about just the, okay, I'll create something that's pretty cool and close and then they don't think about exactly as you described. I have to maintain this thing forever and I have to keep adding features, taking people's feedback. (00:27:13): One of the funniest things that I see again and again, I just had the head of product for Claude Code on the podcast, Cat Wu, and she talks about how Slack is basically the OS for Anthropic. Everything runs through Slack. And you think of all companies that would just like, "We'll just build our own. What are we doing with Slack?" No, they're using Slack like crazy. And I think that's just one example of nobody wants to rebuild a tool like Slack and Workday, I think is another example.
turns.zh: 我完全赞同。我觉得人们往往只想“嗯，造个挺酷的工具，差不多就行了”，却忽视了你刚才提到的深层考量。比如，要永远维护这个工具，不断添加功能，收集用户反馈。（00:27:13）我反复遇到的一个趣事是，我在播客上采访了Claude Code的产品负责人，Cat Wu。她提到Slack基本上是Anthropic的操作系统。所有事务都通过Slack处理。你会发现很多公司都想“我们自己做一个，干嘛还要用Slack？”但实际上，他们疯狂使用Slack。Workday也是个例子。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I don't know. I think it's maybe even more unique in the US, but one of the great things about the US is actually specialization. It's that I get to spend dollars on something like Notion because it's not that expensive compared to me building it and then why would I waste my time? I want to do other things with my life. So I don't know, that's not going to go away.
turns.zh: 我不知道。我觉得这在美国可能更独特，但美国的伟大之处在于专业化。也就是说，我可以花钱买像Notion这样的产品，因为相较于自己开发它，成本并不高——何必浪费时间呢？我还想做其他事情。所以我不知道，这种情况不会消失。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I agree. No, people at Anthropic, their time is better spent on building AGI than trying to build better Slack.
turns.zh: 是啊，我同意。没错，Anthropic的团队把时间花在构建通用人工智能（AGI）上比试图改进Slack更有意义。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I also love the Slack example because, I mean, there's this graphic of what it takes to deliver a notification in Slack, the decision flow chart. And that is just something that you only get to when you have real users, real scale and decades of just, yep, we understand the customer.
turns.zh: 我也很喜欢Slack这个例子。我的意思是，Slack里有个图表，展示了在Slack里发送通知需要经历哪些步骤，还有决策流程图。只有当你有真实用户、真正规模化，并且经过数十年积累后，才能理解客户需求。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to how product building is changing and how it's different. I know you've done a lot of different jobs, but your job, I don't know, a couple years ago, what's most changed? What part is most not something you don't do anymore or you do a lot more of now with AI emerging as a big part of your process?
turns.zh: 我想谈谈产品开发方式的变化和不同之处。我知道你做过很多不同的工作，但你的工作，嗯，几年前，最大的变化是什么？随着AI成为流程的重要组成部分，你不再做某些事，或者现在做得更多了？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I think the first 10% of every project are now free. That's how I would describe it. So there is no point for most things to, for example, write a ... I don't know. The thing has changed. I've never really been great at this, but there's no point in writing a PRD if you can just do the janky version and do the, "Here's the demo of what I think we should build."
turns.zh: 我觉得现在每个项目的前10%都是免费的。这就是我的看法。所以对于大多数事情来说，比如写PRD（产品需求文档），现在已经没必要了。你可以直接做一个粗糙的版本，然后说：“这是我认为我们应该开发的产品演示。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the first 10%, that's so interesting. That's such an interesting way to frame it. Idea, there's just the thinking through of it, you can go a lot further really quickly.
turns.zh: 所以前10%太有意思了。这是一种很有趣的框架。想法阶段，你可以很快探索得更深入。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Yes. And if you look at a lot of the ... It takes almost no effort to now build the first version of a startup or the first version 0.8. And then I think the last, or maybe even if you're generous and say the first 90% are now done, the last 10% are still actually 90%. That's always the hardest. (00:29:42): So I think it's cheaper to just explore a lot of paths. You can now afford to say, "I'm going to send off 10 agents to explore 10 different things and then see if I was right." We used to say this at GitHub in our product reviews a lot, which is demos not memos. And then we would say, give me something to react to, which is, okay, if you're going to write a PRD, just write the change log or the blog post that a user would read. (00:30:10): Now, it's much easier to give people something to react to. As in, yeah, here's the version of the product. And it's like, okay, what if we did it this other way? Oh yeah, here's that version. And so I think that is just amazing. It sort of builds in iteration into the product much earlier. Waterfall is sort of, why bother?
turns.zh: 是的。如果你看看很多……现在开发一家初创公司的第一个版本，或者0.8版本，几乎不需要什么努力了。然后我觉得最后10%，或者即使你大方点说前90%现在也完成了，最后10%仍然占90%。这永远是最难的部分。（00:29:42）：所以我觉得探索多种可能性成本更低了。现在你可以负担得起让10个开发者去探索10种不同的方案，然后看看是否正确。我们在GitHub的产品评审中常说这句话，叫“演示而非备忘录”。然后我们会说，给我点能做出反应的东西。比如，如果你要写PRD，就写变更日志或者用户会读的博客文章。（00:30:10）：现在让人们有反应的机会容易多了。比如，嗯，这是产品版本。然后再问，哦，如果我们换种方式呢？哦，好的，这是另一个版本。所以我觉得这太棒了。它让产品迭代更早地融入其中。瀑布式开发真是没必要了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you think is the next leap or shift in how we build? What are you seeing as like, okay, this is now the new thing that's emerging that is going to change how we operate?
turns.zh: 你认为下一步的飞跃或转变会在哪里？你看到哪些新兴事物会改变我们的运营方式？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I'm very conflicted on this because on one hand, I do want to ... I believe the never bet against plain text. So a famous forum post at some point. Plain text, markdown. It's just such a durable thing. Code is such a durable thing. I think that expressing your thoughts in code is probably a really good thing. We can talk about why. But at the same time, I'm like, are we really going to just be chatting back and forth? (00:31:05): And so what is the future of Figma, for example, is a really interesting example to me because on one hand, I do see a drop in usage of Figma in some designers at Notion. And then others are like, "Nope, these AI tools are wonderful." It's very hard for me to predict of like, is direct manipulation going away because the agent is doing the direct manipulation? (00:31:29): The other thing that I'm curious about is there is this automation versus augmentation fork. If I look at the really, really fast models like Spark, and I forget what the Anthropic variant is where-
turns.zh:
关于这件事，我内心很矛盾。一方面，我确实想……我坚信永远不要与纯文本作对。这曾是某个论坛帖子里的名言。纯文本、Markdown，它们就是如此经久不衰。代码也是如此耐用。用代码来表达想法，或许是个非常好的主意。我们可以探讨其中的缘由。但与此同时，我又在想，我们真的要一直这样你来我往地聊天吗？（00:31:05）  
举个例子，Figma的未来走向对我来说是个很有趣的案例。一方面，我确实看到Notion平台上有些设计师减少了对Figma的使用。而另一些人却说：“不，这些AI工具太棒了。”我很难预测，直接操作功能是否会因为代理程序的介入而消失？（00:31:29）  
另一个让我好奇的点是自动化与增强型工具之间的分野。如果我看那些速度极快的模型，比如Spark，还有Anthropic变体——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Haiku.
turns.zh: 俳句。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: No. Sorry. You still get a smart one. It's Opus, but Opus Fast or something where you-
turns.zh: 不，对不起。你还是能得到智能结果。是Opus，但可能是Opus Fast之类的，你可以——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:31:52]
turns.zh: [00:31:52的不可听清内容]

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: ... very quickly run up a bill of $3,000 a day. But the speed of inference really changes things. If the inference is slow, then you're queuing up a bunch of jobs and then you're walking around the building thinking about other things and then come back and review. Versus if it's nearly instant, are you still going to do this? Is this multitasking the frenetic thing that we currently have going on actually the thing that gives us flow state? Well, no. But if the inference becomes instant, do we get back to direct manipulation? Do you instantly mold the clay that is the code? I don't know. I think it depends on model capabilities, which is do people ... Is there a saturation on intelligence or not? (00:32:41): The analogy I like to give is a retina display, which is after I can't see the pixels, I can't see the pixels. I don't need you to make them smaller. Is it not the same for a lot of cognitive tasks, which is at some sort of level of intelligence? I don't need more and instead I want a different modality and faster. So I don't know. Those things I'm excited about.
turns.zh:
……很快就会产生每天3000美元的账单。但推理速度的提升确实会改变局面。如果推理速度很慢，你就得排队处理一堆任务，然后在办公室里走来走去思考其他事情，最后再回来检查结果。而如果推理速度接近即时，你还会继续这样做吗？这种疯狂的多任务处理方式，实际上是否能让我们进入心流状态？不。但如果推理速度变得即时了，我们会不会回归到直接操作模式？你能立即塑造代码这块“黏土”吗？我不知道。这取决于模型的能力，也就是说人们……智能是否会达到饱和？（00:32:41）  
我喜欢举的类比是视网膜显示屏。当我看不到像素时，就看不到像素了。我不需要把它们缩小。很多认知任务不也是如此吗？在某种智能程度上，我们不需要更多，而是需要不同的交互方式和更快的速度。所以我不知道。这些东西让我很兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. So the last point you're making is it's like smarter models will not significantly impact how teams operate because they've gotten so good and it's other blockers now like UX essentially.
turns.zh: 有意思。所以你最后的观点是，更智能的模型不会显著影响团队的运作方式，因为它们已经变得非常强大，而现在的阻碍因素更多是用户体验等其他方面。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Yeah. I think in general, I'm actually very curious. The labs operate ... I feel like they operate under the assumption that people will always want the smartest model. You want the frontier model. And I think for certain domains, that is probably true. I think if we're going to do cancer research and so on, and if we're going to spend millions of dollars on something, that's likely true. But that's not how we run companies either. We don't have a PhD for everything. And so I think for a lot of knowledge work tasks probably we'll get to good enough. And once you get to good enough, then you can optimize other things. (00:33:49): They run locally. They're cheaper. They're faster. And I don't know why the absolute intelligence thing doesn't interest me very much. I think society is largely not capped by intelligence. I think Tyler Cowen says something similar. I don't want to put words in his mouth. And so I'm much more interested in the exoskeleton versus the I have a god and a box in some data center somewhere and we're all sort of twiddling our thumbs.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得总的来说，我其实很好奇。实验室的运作……我感觉他们运作时假设人们永远想要最智能的模型。你想要前沿的模型。我认为对于某些领域来说，这可能是真的。比如，如果我们要做癌症研究之类的，如果要在某个项目上花费数百万美元，那这很可能是正确的。但这也不是我们运营公司的方式。我们不可能什么问题都有博士来解决。所以我认为对于很多知识型工作任务，我们可能只需要达到足够好的水平。一旦达到足够好的水平，就可以优化其他方面了。（00:33:49）：它们在本地运行。成本更低。速度更快。我不知道为什么绝对的智能程度对我没那么感兴趣。我认为社会并不受智力水平的限制。泰勒·考恩（Tyler Cowen）也说过类似的观点。我不想曲解他的意思。所以我对外骨骼技术更感兴趣，而不是那种“我有上帝般的能力，把数据存储在某个数据中心，然后大家都在干等着”的方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have a bunch of questions along these lines. So interesting. You talked about how this 1PM is the highest token spender. This is across all of Notion?
turns.zh: 我有一些这方面的疑问。太有趣了。你提到下午1点是代币消费最高的时段。这是Notion平台整体的情况吗？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I would assume this may not include our automatic security vulnerability scanning and bug triaging. It's like when human kicks off [inaudible 00:34:36] jobs. Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我猜这可能不包括我们的自动安全漏洞扫描和漏洞修复功能。就像当人工启动[00:34:36]任务时的情况。是的。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's your policy on token spend? Is it spend as much you want? Here's a limit, everyone. Do you keep track of that report?
turns.zh: 你们对代币消费有什么政策？是想花多少就花多少吗？这里给大家设个限额。你们会追踪这份报告吗？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Given that I don't know what the policy is, I think it is unlimited. I mean, you can imagine at some point there would be, but right now, I think it's just the wrong thing to optimize for. It's like when something new comes along, it's worth letting people explore. I do suspect in 6 to 12 months from now, a lot of companies are going to actually start asking questions around ROI, and I think that will be an uncomfortable conversation for a lot of folks.
turns.zh: 鉴于我不知道具体政策，我觉得应该是无限制的。我的意思是，你可以想象未来某个时候会有限制，但现在来说，优化这个指标意义不大。当新技术出现时，让人们去探索是值得的。我确实怀疑6到12个月后，很多公司会开始真正追问ROI（投资回报率）的问题，对很多人来说这会是一次令人不适的对话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In terms of spend, what are the numbers for say Eric or broadly in terms of spend?
turns.zh: 就消费而言，比如Eric或者更广泛地说，每个人的消费数字是多少？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I am the wrong person to ask.
turns.zh: 我不是合适的询问对象。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. It's just a lot. And then-
turns.zh: 好的。数额确实很大。然后-

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: That is just the ... I would assume they pale in comparison to the folks at OpenAI and Anthropic just by the nature of the work they do and so on. But it is definitely for an individual in the ... I don't even want to put numbers in, but thousands for sure, but maybe tens of thousands. I don't know. It depends. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我觉得光是你作为产品负责人，都不清楚这件事，这就说明我们先别去操心这个了。先看看能做些什么，六个月后再看看ROI是否正向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think just the fact that you're as head of product are not on top of that means that it's just, let's not worry about this. Let's just see what we can do and then in six months, as you said, we'll figure out if this is ROI positive.
turns.zh: 是的。我现在有幸可以不去管这些事。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Yes. I have the luxury to right now not care.
turns.zh: 是的。我现在有时间不去操心这些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And I'm sure someone's looking at it. It's not going to be out of control.
turns.zh: 是的。我相信肯定有人在关注这件事。不会失控的。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Correct.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think there's this big, I don't know, milestone of when does token spend exceed someone's salary. That's something people talk about now more and more, just like, should that be higher than your salary? Should it be lower? How does that all connect?
turns.zh: 我觉得有一个重要的里程碑，那就是代币支出何时会超过某人的薪资。这是人们现在越来越热议的话题，比如，代币支出应该高于你的薪资吗？应该低于你的薪资吗？这两者又有何关联？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Yeah, I think there's a real danger in making the token spend the metric to boast about, which is the same as when people boast about how many lines of code they've written in a day. And I'm like, "Why do you have so many lines of code?" You have, I don't know. (00:36:30): The largest software projects in the world have not that many millions of lines of code. Why are we bragging about that? I don't actually care about how many tokens someone spends. Yeah. It's not a metric that's useful.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得把代币支出当作炫耀的指标是件危险的事，这就跟人们炫耀自己一天写了多少行代码一样。我就会问：“你为什么写那么多代码？”你知道吗，（00:36:30）世界上最大的软件项目也不过几百万行代码。我们为什么要为此炫耀？我其实并不关心某人花了多少代币。是啊，这根本不是一个有用的指标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Such a good point. I know Meta got some flak for this recently where they're trying to create a leaderboard of who's doing the most.
turns.zh: 说得太好了。我知道Meta最近因为这事备受指责，他们试图创建一个排行榜，看看谁做得最多。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: To be fair, I do understand why companies do that, which is I am surprised by how much work it takes to get people to identify the outer loop of their work and enlist an agent and build the ... I don't know. The term right now is like factory, like the software factory for the work that they do. It is surprising to me how much prodding you need to do to get people out of the way they're used to working. (00:37:23): And so if you're dealing with tens of thousands of people at the scale of Meta, I have some sympathy for, okay, a good way to do this is just start a leaderboard and encourage people to do it. They will find good things and useful things to do with that as they learn. Yeah.
turns.zh: 说实话，我理解公司这么做的原因。我很惊讶，要让人们意识到工作的外部循环，招募一个代理并搭建……我不知道。现在常用的术语是"软件工厂"，指的是他们所做工作的流程。在我看来，要让人们摆脱习惯的做事方式，需要大量督促。（00:37:23）而当你面对像Meta这样数万人的规模时，要想让他们接受这种改变，就必须采取强硬手段。比如建立排行榜，鼓励人们参与。随着他们不断学习，他们会找到有用的东西。这很有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's such a good point. You have to over-index to change people's default easy behavior. I'm just going to write these periods the way I've always done it. I've gone in the meetings the same way I've done it. I think that makes a lot of sense. (00:37:52): What have you seen actually work with a Notion to get people to significantly change the way they work?
turns.zh: 说得太对了。你必须采取过度激励的措施来改变人们的默认行为。我还是会按自己一贯的方式写这些句号，参加会议也保持原来的习惯。我觉得这很有道理。（00:37:52）在Notion上，实际上，对于离工程部门较远的角色，你不必费太多口舌去说服他们，因为他们会说：“哇，我现在有超能力了。看看我刚建的这个神奇东西。”因为他们之前和之后能做的事情能力差距太大了，这让人兴奋不已。而对于工程部门，西蒙经常提到的一点是，任何手动干预代码的行为都是糟糕的。你很可能在可验证性循环和软件工厂环节出了问题。当然，代码评审除外。我仍然坚持这个观点：你应该多评审代码，而不是把精力花在评审代码上。但至少在编码方面，任何人工干预都应该像发现一个bug一样。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Depends on the role. So roles that are perhaps further away from engineering, actually, you don't have to convince them all that much because they're like, "Whoa, I have superpowers now. Look at this amazing thing I've just built" because the capability gap of what they were able to do before versus after is so huge that it's intoxicating. And then you have to actually almost do the opposite, which is like, yes, but do you understand why we can't merge this PR? (00:38:23): I think on the engineering side, something that Simon last talks about a lot is any manual intervention in code is bad. You probably did something wrong in the verifiability loop and in the software factory. This excludes obviously reviewing code. I am still very much in camp. You should probably review more code than put more effort into reviewing code than you do, but at least on the writing side, every time there is an intervention, a human intervention, it should feel a little bit like a bug. (00:39:00): I think that's a good litmus test for how, I don't know, agent-filled you are.
turns.zh: 我想再谈谈你们使用的工具。你提到Figma在设计部门正逐渐失宠，这真的很有意思。你们团队的工具栈中，有什么工具在兴起，有什么工具在衰落？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to the tools that you use. You mentioned Figma is trending down within the design org, which is really interesting. Is there anything that's trending up, anything else that's trending down in terms of tools in the tool stack of your team?
turns.zh: 我想回到你们使用的工具上。你提到Figma在设计团队中逐渐失宠，这真的很有意思。还有其他工具在你们团队的工具栈中兴起或衰落吗？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: So I'm actually not positive that Figma is trending down. I think it's more that there's two camps. I could totally believe the Jevons paradox, which is Figma is actually going up. And then of course, vibe coding is going up. I don't want to create ... In general, I really, really dislike the rivalry discourse that exists in Silicon Valley, which is for Anthropic to win, OpenAI needs to lose and vice versa and that kind of thing. So I don't want to perpetuate that with the Figma versus coding. (00:39:53): I think the terminal is actually surprising, which is it's initially scary for people and you could do so much, but now PMs are slowly ... Once they're in Claude Code or Codex, everything is fine. And I generally encourage them to not use the GUIs. I encourage them to use the TUIs because I just know that over time they're going to be curious and pull at other threads. And one day they wake up and they're like, "Oh, I understand more of the substrate of how computers work."
turns.zh: 实际上，我并不认为Figma正在走下坡路。我认为更多的是存在两个阵营。我完全可以相信杰文斯悖论，即Figma实际上在崛起。当然，Vibe Coding也在上涨。我不想参与这种竞争论调——比如在硅谷，人们总想让Anthropic赢，OpenAI输，反之亦然。这类争斗我不想延续到Figma与编码之争中。（00:39:53）：我认为终端实际上令人惊讶，最初它让人们感到害怕，功能强大，但现在产品经理们逐渐适应了Claude Code或Codex，一切都变得正常了。我通常鼓励他们不要使用图形用户界面，而是使用文本用户界面，因为我知道随着时间推移，他们会好奇并探索其他功能。终有一天他们会醒悟，"哦，我对计算机底层原理有了更深的理解。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so interesting. So the designers are using the terminal?
turns.zh: 这太有趣了。那么设计师们也在使用终端吗？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Yes. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so cool.
turns.zh: 太酷了。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: And then, I don't know, a conductor is another one. They're basically just mostly using developer tools. It's not that different from what developers use.
turns.zh: 然后，我不知道，指挥者也是另一个群体。他们基本上主要使用开发者工具。这和开发者使用的工具没有太大区别。

turns.zh:
我很兴奋能向你们介绍本季的支持赞助商Vanta。Vanta帮助超过15,000家公司，如Cursor、Ramp、Duolingo、Snowflake和Atlassian，通过AI赢得并证明客户的信任。得益于AI，团队正在比以往更快地构建和发布产品。但因此，产品和业务中引入的风险比以往任何时候都高。
