（00:42:04）：您认为AI接下来会改变哪个角色？是市场营销？是增长？是销售？是设计？除了工程领域，您觉得还有哪些领域开始真正发生变化？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Okay. This is maybe a hot take and I actually don't have enough ... It's very likely that the labs are like, "Ha ha, look at this guy." My take, it's very clear at least empirically that models are getting better at coding at some exponential rate. And I don't think that's changing. (00:42:34): Now, I'm not that impressed with the progress in any other domain. It tends to be ... I don't think they've gotten significantly better at writing. I still very much hate reading AI slop writing. But the thing is software, Andreessen, software is eating the world. Well, if the cost of software and creating software and encoding business practices in code, and I just literally mean the old software 1.0 kind of code, then if that cost is very much going to zero, we will just have a lot more of it. And so I think then in that case, it's more that software engineering will go into all the other domains, not necessarily that there is some sort of ... Yeah, I don't know. (00:43:21): Our folks in HR are automating a lot of things because now, they don't have to bug an engineering team to write that code. And so I think that's how it's going. And if you look at when the model companies say, "Oh, we've made great progress in this other non-coding domain," I was like, "You just applied coding principles to this domain, which is wonderful, but that's what it's getting better at." And so I just think software is eating the world is going to accelerate.
turns.zh:
好吧。这或许是个争议性观点，而且我其实没准备好……很可能那些实验室会觉得：“哈哈，看看这家伙。”我的观点是，至少从经验上看，模型在编码方面的能力正以指数级增长。这点毋庸置疑。（00:42:34）：现在，我对其他领域的进展并不太感冒。通常情况是……我觉得他们在写作能力上并没有显著提升。我还是非常讨厌读那些人工智能写出的烂文章。但关键在于软件，安德森，软件正在吞噬世界。好吧，如果软件的成本、开发软件的成本，以及用代码编写商业逻辑的成本——我指的是传统的1.0版本软件代码——如果这些成本趋近于零，我们就会看到软件应用的爆发式增长。所以我认为，在这种情况下，软件工程会渗透到所有其他领域，而不一定意味着会出现某种全新的……嗯，我也不确定。

（00:43:21）：我们的人力资源部门正在自动化很多工作，因为现在他们不需要再去麻烦工程团队写那些代码了。所以我觉得事情正在朝这个方向发展。当那些模型公司声称：“哦，我们在其他非编码领域取得了重大进展。”时，我会想：“你们不过是把编码原则应用到这个领域而已，这固然不错，但这不过是模型正在变强的表现。”所以我认为软件吞噬世界的趋势只会加速。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is a really interesting take. So it's basically software, just the acceleration of software eating the world versus it's like, it's going to now do a different kind of job. This makes me think about the head of product for Codex said the same thing that every agent, there's all these different kinds of agents and his take is every agent that will win is going to be a coding agent that builds the thing it needs versus it's come, it has certain number of capabilities. OpenCloud's such a good example. It's just like, I will build a skill for myself and now I know how to do this thing.
turns.zh: 这真是很有趣的观点。所以基本上就是软件加速吞噬世界，而不是说它会转向其他领域。这让我想起Codex的产品负责人说过同样的话，他说每个智能体，无论是哪种智能体，只要能胜出，就一定是编码智能体，即构建所需功能的智能体，而不是现成的某种功能。OpenCloud就是个很好的例子。就好像，我会为自己开发一个技能，现在我知道怎么做这件事了。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Yes. All agents are also, if you look at all the harnesses, whether it's the open source ones or the ones from the model companies, ours as well, they all resemble a coding agent now.
turns.zh: 是的。所有智能体现在也都是这样，如果你看看所有的框架，无论是开源的还是模型公司的，包括我们自己的，它们现在都像编码智能体了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to come back to the ROI piece. I think this is really interesting. As you said, there's just like, okay, we're going to spend, spend, spend, just see what happens, learn, accelerate, lean into all this stuff. You're saying that in maybe six months, something like that, you think a lot of companies are going to start really looking at the cost here. I know you said you don't like to predict things, but what do you predict is going to start happening?
turns.zh: 我要回到投资回报率的话题。我觉得这真的很有趣。正如你所说，就是不断投入、投入、再投入，看看结果如何，学习、加速、全力投入所有这些事情。你说大概六个月左右，会有很多公司开始真正关注这里的成本问题。我知道你不喜欢预测，但你预测接下来会发生什么？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I probably spend too much time than I should because I have literally zero impact on any of this as how it plays out, but you can imagine a world where the labs, the delta between the labs and open weight models and so on widens. That is a world that I very much don't like because I hate centralization of power. But in that world, I think the labs just get to decide what the world looks like. (00:45:19): I think if that gap doesn't widen, then you will just see a diffusion and people will get very comfortable running their own models, RLing their own models. Like you see this with Cursor, you see this with Intercom, Notion is dabbling in it as well. Use dabbling right now, but obviously at some point we might become more serious about it. And then you have, it may not be the frontier, but for a lot of tasks, it'll be good enough. And so I think in that case, that is just an ROI calculation. That is the, is it cheaper for me to send this task to a smaller model that is cheaper to run where remove the lab profit margin kind of thing? (00:45:57): I think that may happen, but it only happens if there isn't a fast sort of like, oh yeah, the gap is now so big. The other one that's interesting is right now, I think we're actually in one of the luckiest possible timelines, which is we have, at least in the US, three competent labs that are all sort of duking it out at the ... and like who knows, maybe Meta now, so four. Maybe we can make it six at some point. I think I would love a world where we have a dozen frontier models in the US versus having to always rely on other places in the world to do this, but that's pretty good. (00:46:36): If that stopped, I would be somewhat worried. And then it's hard to predict what would happen. But if that doesn't, then I think it's going to look similar to the cloud wars, which is at some point layers commoditize, businesses are not going to want to lock in into one single provider. I don't know. (00:46:57): In the past life, I worked at Heroku and Kubernetes was much more successful than Heroku, even though I think from a user experience perspective, it was much worse. But the delta was Heroku was saying, "Hey, we're going to replace your ops team." And Kubernetes was, "We're going to make your ops team superheroes. And also, we're not going to lock you into a cloud, you can choose." And obviously, that's what businesses want. Businesses want choice. And so I don't know. It's really hard to predict because it depends. So it's so asymmetric in terms of model progress.
turns.zh: 我可能花了太多时间在这上面，因为我对这一切的结果几乎没有任何影响力。但你可以想象这样一个世界：实验室之间的差距、实验室与开源模型之间的鸿沟等等会不断扩大。这样的世界我非常不喜欢，因为我讨厌权力集中。但在这样的世界里，实验室就能决定世界的模样。（00:45:19）我认为如果这种差距不扩大，人们就会看到技术的扩散，大家会更习惯于运行自己的模型、进行自己的强化学习。就像你看到Cursor这样的公司，Intercom、Notion也在尝试。但现在只是尝试，显然未来我们可能会更认真对待它。然后你会发现，虽然这可能不是前沿领域，但对于很多任务来说，它已经足够好了。所以我认为在这种情况下，这就是一个投资回报率的计算。对我来说，把这个任务交给一个更便宜、更易于运行的模型，而不是让实验室赚取利润差，这更划算吗？（00:45:57）我认为这可能会发生，但只有在差距不迅速扩大的情况下才会发生。比如现在，我们实际上处于一个最幸运的时间线：至少在美国，有三个有实力的实验室在激烈竞争……谁知道呢，也许现在Meta也会加入，总共四个。也许未来还能增加到六个。我希望美国能有十几个前沿模型，而不是总是依赖世界其他地区来做这件事，但现状已经很不错了。（00:46:36）如果这种竞争停止，我会有些担心。然后很难预测接下来会发生什么。但如果它不停止，那么我认为它会像云计算之战一样发展。在某个阶段，层级会商品化，企业不会想被锁定在单一供应商上。谁知道呢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you say the products that win often are the ones that make you feel like superheroes, I always think about Kathy Sierra. Do you remember that at all as a thing?
turns.zh: 当你说赢得市场的产品往往是那些让你感觉像超级英雄的产品时，我总会想起凯西·塞拉。你还记得这件事吗？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: It rings a bell.
turns.zh: 这让我想起了一些事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. It's like from the open days at this point shows how old I am. She was just something that really stuck with me and I think it's informed a lot of how people think about product, at least in the past is just her whole pitch was instead of talking about your product and how amazing it is, it's about we'll make you a superhero. It's like Mario getting the little flower and having superpowers now versus look at her incredible product.
turns.zh: 好吧。这让我意识到自己有多老了。她对我来说是一个非常深刻的印象，我认为这影响了人们对产品的思考方式，至少在过去，她的整个理念就是：不要谈论你的产品有多棒，而是要让你们成为超级英雄。这就像马里奥得到小花后获得超能力，而不是去看她那令人惊叹的产品。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I think it's actually a thing that the coding companies had to learn when they tried to move to like, why do code review tools, automatic code review tools not work that well? I think there's actually a subtle thing, which is you push your code publicly to or publicly within your organization or your team, and then a thing roasts your code and tells you how terrible of a developer you are. (00:48:25): Versus if you think about what Claude Code and Codex does is you're coding and then you publish the work of you plus Claude and you get bragging rights of how good of a developer you are. And so I think the superhero stuff is definitely true.
turns.zh: 我觉得这其实是编程公司在尝试迁移到自动代码审查工具时必须面对的一个难题。为什么这些工具效果不佳？我认为问题的关键在于，当你把代码公开推送到组织或团队内部时，它们会严厉批评你的代码，告诉你你是个糟糕的开发者。而Claude Code和Codex则不同——你编写代码后，再发布与Claude合作的成果，就能获得炫耀自己编程能力的资本。所以我认为超级英雄般的体验确实存在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of superhero, I wasn't planning to talk about this, but I've been hearing a lot about how much people love your agent, the Notion AI agent that you all released. It's just coming up a lot of just like, wow, this is actually really useful with a lot of different people. It'd be interesting to hear what you think made it so successful. I know it was a long time before you guys launched it. Just like, what do you think is helping it be this useful and successful as a product out in the world?
turns.zh: 说到超级英雄，我本不打算谈论这个，但我听说很多人对你们推出的Notion AI助手赞不绝口。它确实很受欢迎，许多人对它赞不绝口。能听听你们认为它为何如此成功吗？毕竟推出它花了很长时间。你们觉得是什么让它如此实用且成功？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I would like it to be even better. So I'm like my own first critic, I guess. I've spent most of my day thinking about where it falls short, not how great it is, but I agree with you that I'm actually surprised at how ... This sounds so weird. I'm surprised how good it is, if that makes sense. (00:49:27): Notion has always been fairly at the forefront of AI. I think the first Notion Assistant was actually launched before ChatGPT. And so it's not that ... I think both Ivan and Simon had the intuition of, "Hey, this is going to change a lot of things." And so that's a huge reason why, but every company wants to become AI native now, whatever that means. It's kind of like cloud native. I'm like, "If you have to say it, then are you really, do you have a chance?" But I'm surprised how fast that happened for Notion, and I'll take almost no credit in this. (00:50:00): I think what's good about it is agents need context to operate in. Agents don't really like walls of like, "Oh, I have to go through this narrow orifice to talk to this other data repository." And I think for the first time, it is obvious to people why a connected workspace is actually valuable because it's great. I can have agents roam around and do that. And it touches on malleable software. (00:50:28): I think of Notion as an operating system more so. And then in that case, it resembles the environment that coding agents are in with Unix much more than one might maybe intuitively think. So I think those all contribute. And then sometimes it's just we're just dumb enough to try hard things. And so I think our enterprise search is like this thing where we do a lot of automatic permission handling and so on that others don't. I don't know. You have to care.
turns.zh: 我希望它能更完善。所以我算是自己最严厉的批评者吧。我今天大部分时间都在思考它的缺点，而不是优点。但我同意你的看法，我确实很惊讶它如此出色——这听起来很奇怪。我是说，它真的很棒，如果你能理解的话。（00:49:27）Notion在AI领域一直处于前沿。我记得Notion Assistant实际上是在ChatGPT之前推出的。所以这不是……我觉得Ivan和Simon当时就有预见，"嘿，这将改变很多东西。"这就是它成功的重要原因。但现在每个公司都想实现AI原生化，无论这意味着什么。这有点像云原生。我会想，"如果你非要这么说，那你真的有机会吗？"但Notion的成功速度之快让我很惊讶，对此我几乎不居功。（00:50:00）我认为它的优点在于，智能助手需要上下文才能运行。助手不喜欢面对诸如"哦，我必须穿过这个狭窄的通道才能与其他数据库交谈"这样的障碍。我认为人们第一次意识到互联的工作空间的价值，因为它真的很棒。我可以让助手四处活动。这也涉及到可塑性软件。（00:50:28）我更把Notion视为一个操作系统。在这种情况下，它与Unix环境的相似度远超人们的想象。所以所有这些因素都起到了作用。有时我们就是足够愚蠢，愿意尝试困难的事情。比如我们的企业搜索功能，我们做了很多自动权限处理等其他公司不做的事情。我不知道，但你必须用心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to come back to my quote from the Bible. I feel like that actually is an answer to this question that it was made for such a time as this. The fact that Notion basically has all the things about everything in your company is the perfect source of context for using AI and helping you work. So it's just like just being around long enough for, wow, okay, this is exactly what we've been meant to be. It's a nice job. Nice job, [inaudible 00:51:19].
turns.zh: 我要回到我引用的《圣经》经文了。我觉得这其实是对这个问题的答案，它就是为这样一个时代而设计的。Notion基本上涵盖了公司内所有事务，这为使用AI和协作提供了完美的上下文。所以只要你经历得够久，就会意识到，哇，好吧，这正是我们注定要做的。这是一项很棒的工作。干得好，[00:51:19语音模糊]。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: It's the same as malleable software. I love that people are waking up to malleable software now, but it's been around for a long time. It was just always slightly too hard and slightly too, why would I do this? And so I think, yeah, I'm going to use this quote from the Bible. Thank you.
turns.zh: 这和可塑性软件是一样的。我很高兴现在人们开始意识到可塑性软件的重要性，但这种理念其实由来已久。只是过去它总是显得太难、太让人却步——人们总会想："我为什么要这么做？"所以我觉得，是的，我要引用圣经里的一句话。谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There it is. It's like shorter. The original quote is for such a time as this and interpretation is this you're like destined to do this thing. It's very Bible every episode. Oh man. (00:51:48): Going back to the way your team operates, because I think this is something that a lot of people are thinking about right now. There's all this talk of productivity, pace, getting things out like Anthropics launching a massive product every day, basically. Your job as head of product help people ship consistently, regularly, often ship great stuff. (00:52:05): What has worked in allowing you guys to ship more quickly, if you are, and stuff that you're proud of, stuff that works?
turns.zh:
就是这样。原文是"for such a time as this"，意思是"此刻正是关键时刻"，解读起来就是"你注定要做这件事"。每期节目都充满圣经色彩。天啊。
(00:51:48)：回到你们团队的运作方式，我觉得这是很多人现在都在思考的问题。到处都在谈论生产力、节奏，Anthropics每天发布大型产品之类的。作为产品负责人，您的职责是帮助团队持续、高频地发布优质成果。
(00:52:05)：在帮助团队更快发布、交付令你们自豪且有效的成果方面，哪些方法行之有效？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I think this answer is so specific to companies like internal culture where if you ... I've been in this situation twice in my career. One is when I joined GitHub, which is obviously, I think, I don't know, insane product market fit, it just so happened that at the time that I had joined, there was a little bit of a, I don't know, identity crisis or like, "Oh, what's our next act? What do we do?" And lots of debates about what to ship because it's such a tough act to follow if your first act was just incredible. And I don't know, I would put Notion in the same bucket. (00:52:49): And so in this case, it's just reminding people that, "Hey, you can just do stuff. We don't have to be that precious." I think there's this preciousness that develops over time. It's like, "Oh, what do we do when our users are going to be upset?" Well, our users are going to be upset if we don't innovate more so than if we accidentally break a thing. (00:53:06): So it's obviously a balance, but I think just reminding people that the same group of people that was able to do the first act is very likely going to be able to do the second one, but you have to try. Shots on goal is a thing that we say internally a lot, which is like, great, how do you increase shots on goal? Which of course, if we go back to it's easier to experiment now, you're increasing the shots of on goal. So I think that has worked really well. (00:53:30): Just shipping feature after feature doesn't ... We have been a little bit on a roll in terms of shipping new functionality maybe in the last, I don't know, six months or so. But at the end of the day, feature count is the same silly metric as lines of code or tokens consumed or whatever. I would rather have fewer features that are really, really good and where the combinatorics let you do everything. And so I think something that I'm still very much struggling with is software quality. And I will also say I don't think the labs are exempt from this. (00:54:07): I love their tools. It's great. I live in the CLIs, but a regression every two weeks of a thing that was fixed three weeks before, and they still can't render a TUI at, I don't know, a frame rate that's reasonable. And so I think quality is a thing that's missing. This Apple-esque machined, unibody, aluminum kind of engineering, I would like us to figure out how to get back to that as an industry.
turns.zh:
我觉得这个答案非常针对公司内部文化。如果你……我职业生涯中遇到过两次类似情况。一次是加入GitHub时，那显然是个产品市场契合度极高的案例。但当时我加入时，团队正经历某种身份危机——“接下来该做什么？”。关于发布什么功能的争论很多，因为如果首个版本已经足够惊艳，后续就很难超越了。Notion的情况也类似。
(00:52:49)：所以关键在于提醒人们："嘿，你们大可以放手去做。我们没必要太拘谨。" 我觉得人们会逐渐形成一种谨慎心理。比如"用户会生气吗？"但用户更生气的是我们不创新，而不是偶然出错。平衡很重要，但要让大家知道，首个版本成功的团队很可能能再创辉煌。内部常说"多尝试"，这意味着多尝试，自然就会增加成功概率。
(00:53:30)：连续发布功能未必有效。过去六个月左右我们确实进展不错，但最终衡量标准还是功能数量、代码行数、消耗的token数之类的。我更希望少量高质量功能，组合起来能实现全局。软件质量仍是难题，实验室部门也未能幸免。
(00:54:07)：我爱他们的工具，CLI体验超棒。但每两周就有两周前修复的漏洞回归，图形界面帧率低得离谱。我希望整个行业能重拾苹果式的工程哲学——一体化设计、精工打造。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there something you've done to help improve that? So there's code quality and then there's actual software quality. If you're shipping shots on goal, there's always this balance of, okay, I would wait for it to be awesome. I know this is just very hard question to answer, but just what's your communication to the team of, here's where we're going to find that balance?
turns.zh: 你们有没有采取过什么措施来帮助提升这一点？所以说既有代码质量，也有实际的软件质量。如果你只是在追求速成，那就永远存在一种平衡：好吧，我可以等等让它变得完美。我知道这是一个很难回答的问题，但你如何向团队传达，我们要在这里找到这种平衡？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: And this is a very frustrating thing for people, but actually, I can't show you because I'm using my laptop, but we have obviously good stickers, which is let's just only make obviously good stuff. The origin, which is like, okay, wait, what does that mean? And I'm like, "Ah, you know it when you see it." (00:55:09): I don't think anyone argued when they saw the first iPhone that it's obviously good. I don't think anyone argued that when ChatGPT first came out that it's obviously good. And so I think that's the bar. Just make obviously good stuff. I think the mistake that maybe a lot of companies then make is great, we're going to be in this cave in isolation until we have it be obviously good. (00:55:29): One of my core values is incremental correctness, which is iterate, get really, really good at iterating. And so I don't know, it's probably a union of, okay, increase shots on goal. Here's a great example. We get roasted from our customers all the time, which I love about we have like six automation primitives inside of Notion if you include all the agents and so on. And I'm like, yep, we let a bunch of different ideas grow. We look at how they work, but then you do have to do the hard work at consolidating it back into the naked robotic core of that idea. And that's hard because you have to be okay with perhaps then shipping the next thing slightly delayed as you reconcile. (00:56:11): I don't know. I think we have work to do there at Notion, but as an industry too. Like somebody was joking like, why does Claude, the desktop have three tabs of co-work, code, and I don't know what the first chat or whatever, why do we have six automation primitives? (00:56:27): Well, because someone has to sit down and reconcile them and figure out what's actually the core simple thing that should outlive the other evolutionary branches of that same idea.
turns.zh: 这对人们来说确实很令人沮丧，但实际上，我没法展示给你们看，因为我用的是笔记本电脑，但我们显然有很棒的贴纸，就是只做显然很棒的东西。原点，就是比如，等等，这是什么意思？我会说，"啊，你看到的时候就知道了。"（00:55:09）：我觉得当人们看到第一款iPhone时，没人会质疑它显然很棒。当ChatGPT刚推出时，没人会质疑它显然很棒。所以我认为这就是标准。只做显然很棒的东西。我觉得很多公司可能犯的错误是，嗯，我们要在一个封闭的环境里闭门造车直到它变得显然很棒。（00:55:29）：我的核心价值观之一是渐进式正确性，就是迭代，真正精通迭代。我不知道，这可能是一个综合体，就是增加射正次数。这里有个很好的例子。我们总是被客户吐槽，我很喜欢这一点——如果你把Notion里的所有代理等因素都算进来，我们有六个自动化原语。我会说，没错，我们让很多不同的想法成长起来，看看它们如何运作，但你确实需要下功夫把它们整合回这个想法的核心机器人部分。这很难，因为你必须接受可能因此导致下一次发布稍微延迟的事实。（00:56:11）：我不知道。我觉得Notion还有很多工作要做，但整个行业也是如此。比如有人开玩笑说，为什么Claude桌面版有三个标签页，协作、代码，还有第一个不知道是什么聊天之类的，为什么我们有六个自动化原语？（00:56:27）：嗯，因为总得有人坐下来把它们整合起来，找出真正核心的、能经受住同一想法其他进化分支考验的简单之处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This idea of knowing when things are obviously good, there's an element of having taste, and this is word taste that comes up a lot now, and this is like what we will need more and more because AI is building a thing now. Our job is taste. Is this great? Is this good? (00:56:54): I feel like you're someone that has really great taste. A question people always ask, "How do I build taste? Do I have taste?" Do you have any advice for someone that's like, "I want to develop my taste"?
turns.zh: 这种知道何时东西显然很棒的理念，包含了品味的元素，而“品味”这个词现在被提得很多。这是我们越来越需要的东西，因为AI正在构建一个体系。我们的工作就是品味。这很棒吗？这好吗？（00:56:54）：我觉得你是一个品味很棒的人。人们常问的一个问题是，“如何培养品味？我有品味吗？”对于那些想培养品味的人，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: First of all, I don't know if I have great taste. I look at others and I look at how they exercise tastes. And I think that the common thing I think is iterations with feedback. So it takes a really long time to build up taste in a specific domain. Then you maybe often can extrapolate into other domains with that taste. But if I had to describe what taste actually means, it's you're able to run, this is such a nerdy way of describing it, you're able to run a virtual machine in your head where given an idea, you can predict for a certain in group whether they're going to like it or not. (00:57:48): The extremes are is, if you are the only person on the planet that thinks something is good, is it good? No. But maybe you also don't need to build a product for eight billion people. I've never built consumer software. I would probably be terrible at it, but you decide what your in group is and then how good do you get at emulating how they will react to it. (00:58:11): And to do that, you just have to do reps. It's almost like training a model, which is also why I'm not super ... You know the whole, "Ooh, the one thing that we have left is taste." I'm not so sure. If you think about the loop, it's input idea, how do people react? That seems very back propagation. I don't know. It seems very much how we train models too.
turns.zh: 首先，我不知道自己是否有很好的品味。我观察别人，看他们如何培养品味。我认为一个共性是不断迭代并获取反馈。所以在某个特定领域培养品味需要很长时间。然后，你或许能将这种品味延伸到其他领域。但如果让我解释品味到底意味着什么，那就是你要能够运行一个虚拟的大脑模拟：当给定一个创意时，你能预测某个特定群体是否会喜欢它。（00:57:48）：极端情况是，如果你是地球上唯一认为某样东西好的人，那它真的好吗？不。但或许你也不需要为80亿人开发产品。我从未开发过消费级软件，我可能做得很糟糕。但你要确定自己的目标群体，然后尽可能模仿他们的反应方式。（00:58:11）：要做到这一点，就必须不断练习。这几乎就像训练模型一样，这也是我不太认同“品味是我们剩下的唯一东西”这种观点的缘由。我认为品味的培养本质上就是不断实践、获取反馈、迭代的过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I love, basically you build taste by just doing the thing, getting feedback, iterating.
turns.zh: 所以我喜欢的方式，基本上就是通过实际操作、获取反馈、不断迭代来培养品味。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Look at Japan, like Japanese craftspeople, right? They've just been, I don't know, painting the bowl for however long and it just takes a while. And so I think the more reps, the increase the frequency of reps, that's what I would say.
turns.zh: 看看日本，比如日本工匠，对吧？他们一直在画碗，不知道做了多久，这就是个漫长的过程。所以我认为练习的次数越多，反馈越频繁，这才是关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so funny. That's exactly how agents learn and develop how, as you said, models learn just like doing the thing, seeing was this good, was this correct? No. Okay, learn. So it's just doing the thing, learning, getting feedback, and there's no way to speed around this. This is why often people with the best taste have been doing this for a long time.
turns.zh: 太有趣了。这正是代理学习和模型训练的思路——就像你说的，模型通过实践、观察结果、调整策略来学习。没有捷径。这就是为什么品味高超的人往往需要长期积累经验。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: The one thing I will say that I've noticed is specifically for designers, the designers that I think have, at least in software design, high taste are the ones that both have side projects that they build where they're responsible of the full thing and extent. And they're also always tinkering with some new app. (00:59:33): They're the annoying person that is like, "Hey, what if we tried this in our team?" And I'm like, "Really, this is the 49th time that you suggested in a tool. Do we really need this?" It's exposure to other people's ideas. I think that is the ... It's also really important to surround yourself with tasteful things so that you feel like the thing you are making is lacking. (00:59:53): One of the things we do at Notion is all of our conference rooms are named after famous objects like The first typewriter, the Macintosh, a Porsche 911 and so on. And so inevitably when I'm sitting in one of the rooms and I pay attention to the room, nothing I'm doing amounts to this. I got to do better.
turns.zh: 我注意到的一个现象是，特别是设计师方面，至少在软件设计领域，品味出众的设计师往往既有个人项目，完全负责项目的全过程，又不断尝试新应用。（00:59:33）：他们就是那种烦人的家伙，总是说：“嘿，我们团队试试这个吧？”我就会说：“真的吗？这已经是你第49次提议这个工具了。我们真的需要它吗？”这就是接触他人想法的意义。我认为周围有品味高超的人很重要，这样你会觉得自己做的作品有所欠缺。（00:59:53）：我们Notion公司所有会议室都以著名物品命名，比如第一台打字机、Macintosh、保时捷911等等。每次坐在这些会议室里，我都会审视房间环境，发现自己的工作远不及它们的成就。我得做得更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've built so many successful, great, loved products. What do you think matters in the end to building a successful product if you had to just boil it down?
turns.zh: 你开发了许多成功、出色、深受用户喜爱的产品。如果要归结为一个要素，你认为打造成功产品的关键是什么？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Yes. Here's the one trick that I'll sell a course next week.
turns.zh: 是的。下周我要开一门课程，专门传授这个技巧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Please, I'll sign up.
turns.zh: 拜托，我要报名了。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: First of all, I think I would actually say that I have contributed to some really great products, not built them because I think I did not use to believe this early on in my career, but the longer I'm in this, the more I care about what's the team that's building the thing. I used to think that was such a, I don't know, not important thing. And now I'm like, oh, it's the only thing. (01:00:52): I don't think that there is a through line out of the things that I've contributed to where I can pinpoint it. I think that you can't say that the best design always wins. I think there's many products where just design doesn't matter. And I think then as a designer, you can have this identity crisis of like, why am I doing this? I think you can't even say that the way it's built always, the best engineering always wins. (01:01:15): I think one of the biggest pitfalls is if you get into the loop of, if I just add one more thing to the product, it'll be finally great. If I really look at the truly great products, they all have one tiny core that is so exceptionally good. And that is both a combination of you stumbled upon it by luck and then the market agreed. But I think it's the, what's the tiny core? I don't know, multi-touch on the phone. (01:01:43): GitHub is probably the poll request. This idea that anyone can suggest something to you and you see it. I do think that at Notion, it's the blocks and the slash commands. Figma, it's the seamless blend between real-time collaboration and not. All the great products have something tiny that is a superpower that's like versus, oh yeah, if we have this suite of things and we add one more thing, it'll finally be useful. That never works.
turns.zh: 首先，我觉得我其实会说，我参与过一些非常出色的产品，但我并没有亲自开发它们，因为我觉得在职业生涯早期我并不这么认为，但随着从业时间越长，我越关注开发团队的质量。我曾经认为这不是什么重要的事情。现在我觉得，这才是唯一重要的。（01:00:52）：我觉得我参与过的产品中，没有一条能让我明确指出其成功的关键因素。我认为不能说设计总是能胜出。很多产品的设计根本无关紧要。作为设计师，你可能会陷入身份认同危机，比如我为什么要做这个？我甚至不能说技术实现总是能胜出。（01:01:15）：我认为最大的陷阱之一是，如果你陷入这样的循环：只要再给产品添加一个功能，它就能最终变得出色。如果我看看真正伟大的产品，它们都有一个极其出色的核心功能。这既是偶然的发现，也是市场的认可。但我认为，这个核心功能是什么？我不知道，比如手机上的多点触控。（01:01:43）：GitHub可能是投票请求功能。任何人都能向你提出建议，你就能看到这些建议。我认为Notion的核心是块状元素和斜杠命令。Figma是实时协作与非实时协作之间的无缝衔接。所有伟大的产品都有一个微小的核心功能，它就像是一种超能力，而不像是说"如果我们拥有这套功能，再添加一个功能，它最终就能派上用场"。这种方法永远行不通。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And for GitHub, interesting, it was the PR. Are there examples of that at other places you worked? Because this is really interesting, just like what's the tiny core that makes everything else work?
turns.zh: 说到GitHub，有趣的是，是PR功能。在其他你工作过的公司，有没有类似的例子？因为这真的很有趣，什么样的微小核心功能能让其他一切运转起来？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: At Heroku, for sure, I think it was the Git Push Heroku master of ... at the time it was really hard to deploy apps. It's sad because people don't remember Heroku. I have to explain it as it's the Vercel. It's the first Vercel.
turns.zh: 在Heroku方面，肯定是Git Push Heroku主分支功能……当时部署应用程序非常困难。可惜的是，人们已经不记得Heroku了。我得解释说它就是Vercel的原型，是第一个Vercel。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did it get bought by Salesforce? Who bought ...
turns.zh: 是的。是的。是的。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Yes. Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。是的。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Yeah. Git Push Heroku master was just this very simple one-liner that went from the thing on my computer, now I have a URL, and that's so intoxicating that everything else flows from there. (01:02:57): Dropbox is a great one. I think Dropbox is such an interesting study where it was the little menu bar icon that was so good at syncing that you could even use it as a symbol for, do I have internet or not? Because it was better at figuring out whether you had an internet connection than your Mac itself. And it was just, that's the job. Get out of the way and just all my files are always there. And then for years, they've tried to increase the surface area. And I kept thinking, "No, no, no, push it back. I don't want more. This is the only job I want from you. And so I think the tiny core is the thing that makes great products.
turns.zh: 对。Git Push Heroku主分支功能就是这么简单的一个命令行，它把我电脑上的代码直接推送到Heroku主分支。这种感觉太棒了，其他一切都顺理成章了。（01:02:57）：Dropbox是个很好的例子。我认为Dropbox是一个很有趣的案例，它就是那个小小的菜单栏图标，在同步文件方面做得非常好，甚至可以用它来判断自己是否有网络连接，因为它比Mac本身更能准确判断是否有网络连接。这就是核心功能：不碍事，所有文件随时可用。而多年来，他们一直试图增加功能覆盖面。我一直说：“不，不，不，退回去。我不需要更多功能。这就是我唯一的要求。”所以我认为微小的核心功能才是伟大产品的关键所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And Snapchat, obviously, just the disappearing photo concept is so interesting. I heard you've also talk about just being first doesn't matter that much either.
turns.zh: 显然，Snapchat的消失照片功能非常有趣。我听说你还提到，先行者优势未必那么重要。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: You have to be right, not first. I don't know. I mean, there are elements of, if you talk about network effects and perhaps now with training models, it doesn't make sense if you have a headstart, but I think it's overrated. I don't know. (01:04:02): My favorite example is like Bluetooth headphones were crappy and then you have the AirPods and like, oh, they connect and so on. And they weren't the first. I don't know. They weren't the first MP3 player. They weren't the first. You just got to do it right. I don't think being first is all that useful. (01:04:17): I think we're currently, because it's so hard to keep people's attention, we're like, "Oh, how do I go viral? How do I do the Cluely thing?" And I'm like, "Yep, durability matters." Think of like, how would you build Ikea like a generational company that is not concerning itself with whatever is trending on Twitter today?
turns.zh:
你必须做得正确，而非先行。我不知道。我的意思是，如果你谈论网络效应，或许现在涉及训练模型，先行者优势确实没那么重要，但我觉得这被高估了。我不知道。（01:04:02）：我最喜欢的例子是蓝牙耳机一开始质量很差，然后有了AirPods，人们会说，哦，它能连接之类的。但它们并非先行者。它们不是首款MP3播放器，也不是先行者。你只需把事情做对。我认为先行者没那么有用。
（01:04:17）：我认为目前，由于留住用户注意力太难，我们总在想，“哦，如何走红？如何效仿Cluely的做法？”而我会说，“是啊，耐久性才是关键。” 想想看，你如何打造像宜家这样的百年企业，而不去追逐当下Twitter上的流行趋势？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think speaking of models, a good example is Anthropic, which was way behind, started after OpenAI, got less funding and now is just killing it and dominating.
turns.zh: 说到模型，一个很好的例子是Anthropic，它落后很多，成立于OpenAI之后，获得的资金也较少，但现在却大获成功。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: The thing that I find the most impressive about ... I don't know who to give credit, but obviously, you give the CEO a bunch of credit, but like Dario is that he wasn't ... Oh, he wasn't just lucky once at OpenAI. He did the same thing twice and it was successful twice. And I think that's actually really cool.
turns.zh: 我觉得最令人印象深刻的是……我不知道该把功劳归给谁，但显然你会给CEO很多赞誉，但达里奥（Dario）不是……哦，他在OpenAI并非仅有一次幸运。他做了两次相同的事，两次都成功了。我觉得这真的很酷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know you're also a believer in jobs to be done as a way of thinking about product, which it's been a long time controversial topic on this podcast mostly because of Sriram who's very anti-jobs to be done. What's your framing of how you find this framework useful in thinking about product?
turns.zh: 我知道你也相信“工作要完成”这一产品设计框架。这一框架在本播客中长期存在争议，主要因为斯里拉姆（Sriram）非常反对它。你如何看待这个框架在产品设计中的实用性？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I bet that if I reread all of the Clayton Christensen stuff, I would also not identify super strongly with it. I use it mostly as, have you thought holistically about what the user wants to hire your product for? And are you honest about what the user wants versus what you want the user to want? (01:05:48): And then the other thing that I find happens very frequently in larger organizations is that people turn off the brain when they're reviewing their own products from a, "I'm a user, is this a good experience?" And they're more like, "I'm an employee of this company and I made a thing." And so I think jobs to be done might encourage people to zoom out and not get lost in the sauce of making the thing. That's why I like the framework. It's a good reminder of like, no, no, no, no. (01:06:23): The user hires you for a thing, be that user for a second. Would you even buy the thing that you just made? And the answer often is like, "Oh, I hadn't thought about that." And so that's how I use it.
turns.zh: 我敢打赌，如果我重读克莱顿·克里斯滕森（Clayton Christensen）的所有著作，我也不会完全认同。我主要用它来思考：你是否全面考虑了用户雇佣你的产品来做什么？你是否诚实地面对用户的需求与你自己的需求之间的差异？（01:05:48）：然后我在大型组织中经常遇到的情况是，人们在评估自己的产品时，会关闭大脑，脱离“我是用户，这是一个好的体验？”的视角，而是更像是“我是这家公司的员工，我做出了一个东西”。所以我认为“工作要完成”框架可能会鼓励人们退后一步，不迷失在制作产品的过程中。因此我喜欢这个框架。它是一个很好的提醒，别忘了用户雇佣你是为了做某件事，你得暂时把自己当成用户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of this from some of the products you worked on just to make this real for people other than Milkshake example, obviously?
turns.zh: 除了Milkshake的例子外，还有其他你参与过的产品能让人们更直观理解这一点吗？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: There's a very recent one which is more about communication. We're launching a new feature soon and we're working on this landing page to describe the feature. And I found that when people make landing pages, first of all, their writing skills just deteriorate immediately because they want to sound clever and marketing speak comes out of their mouth. And I'm like, "Wait, that's not how you would explain it to a friend." (01:07:02): And then if I'm communicating this product to you, just pretend you're standing in front of a whiteboard. What's the manic thing that you're drawing on the whiteboard to communicate this versus, okay, now go back to the thing you just designed, look at it? Are you telling me that those are the same thing? Are you telling me that you understand what this thing does and that zoom out? So I don't know. Yeah, I don't know. I don't want to pick on individual recent things though.
turns.zh:
最近有个案例，重点在于沟通。我们很快要推出一项新功能，目前正在制作登陆页面来介绍这个功能。我发现人们在制作登陆页面时，首先写作能力会急剧下降，因为他们想显得很聪明，结果说出的话都是营销术语。我就想：“等等，这可不是跟朋友解释产品该有的语气。”（01:07:02）  
然后如果我要向你介绍这个产品，就假设你站在白板前。白板上画着什么夸张的图形来传达信息，还是直接回归到你刚设计好的页面看看呢？你告诉我这两者是一样的吗？你告诉我你理解这个功能，还能放大缩小？所以我不知道。是啊，我不知道。不过我不想针对最近的个别案例。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. As we close out this conversation, there's something I want to get here. You have this hot take on universal basic income. It's completely out of the blue, but I think it's interesting to hear. There's this idea that with AI emerging, we may not need to work. We'll just get some UBI and enjoy our life and you have this hot take that maybe we already have universal basic income. What's going on?
turns.zh: 好的。在结束这次对话时，我想提一下你对全民基本收入的看法。这完全出乎意料，但我觉得挺有意思的。有人认为随着人工智能兴起，我们可能无需工作，只需领取全民基本收入，享受生活。而你却说我们可能已经拥有全民基本收入了。怎么回事？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Yeah. So please extend me some grace here because I both mean it as a joke and maybe somewhat real, just depends on which altitude of human nature you look at. My take is that we already have universal basic income. It's called knowledge work. And I don't exclude my job from it, but if you really look at what do we actually need to live and like to be content, it is a lot less. (01:08:15): And we've built this hierarchy and all these jobs and all these things that are absolutely necessary. And so to me it's like, yeah, we already have it. It's UBI and we'll come up with other ways in which we as humans, because we're the most important species in the universe, insert ourselves into the conversation around agents. (01:08:35): Will it look the same? I don't know. But yeah, I don't know. We are so inventive and we come up with new reasons of why we absolutely must be in that loop. And so I think that's my hot take.
turns.zh:
是的。请别介意我的玩笑话，也许还有点认真，这取决于你如何看待人性。我的观点是，我们已经有全民基本收入了。这叫知识工作。我不排除我的工作也在其中，但如果你仔细想想，真正维持生活和获得满足感所需的东西其实很少。（01:08:15）  
我们建立了层层等级，创造了各种必不可少的工作岗位。所以在我看来，没错，我们已经拥有了全民基本收入。这就是全民基本收入，而我们人类作为宇宙中最重要的物种，会想方设法把自己插入到智能体的对话中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: People have always joked, we get paid so much just to sit in front of a computer and put the right sorts of words and letters into this thing and we get paid a lot of money to do it. And now it's like, oh shit, maybe I won't be paid this much in the future because AI is going to be taking over. And so your take there is just like, this is a pretty sweet gig we already got. Enjoy this UBI.
turns.zh: 人们总是开玩笑说，我们只需坐在电脑前输入正确的字母和单词就能赚大钱。现在却担心AI接管后未来的收入可能大幅降低。所以你的观点就是，我们现在的工作已经很不错了。好好享受全民基本收入吧。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Yes. I think all things considered, how lucky are we? I don't know. I'm sitting in an air-conditioned room right now talking to you, having a good time. I don't know. Yeah. (01:09:19): Just to be clear, not everybody has that luck, but I think that's the folks that I find discussing this the most are the ones that are in the bucket of luck.
turns.zh:
是的。综合来看，我们有多幸运呢？我不知道。我现在坐在有空调的房间里跟你聊天，还挺开心的。我不知道。是啊。（01:09:19）  
不过要说清楚，不是每个人都这么幸运，但我发现讨论这个话题的人大多属于幸运的那一群。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Say we have AGI, you don't have to work, you could just do anything. What would you be spending your time doing?
turns.zh: 假设我们有了通用人工智能，你无需工作，想做什么都可以。那你会怎么安排时间呢？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I actually ask this to almost everybody that we hire. I would be doing the exact same thing. I would probably spend less time having meetings and managing. One of the sad things about my job is that I have yet to replace 80% of it with agentic loops. I envy our engineers and designers who get to do this. So hopefully at some point I won't have a job, but yeah, I would do the same thing. (01:10:04): I think I am someone who I don't code because of a utility. I code because it's also an intellectual challenge. So I think of it as playing chess and Go. I'm very sad that Lee Sedol, after losing against, I think ... I don't know if it's AlphaGo or Zero, but one of the two. It seems like he gave up on Go. And I'm like, who cares if some machine is better at it? It's the human stuff. Just keep going at it. And so I think I would do the same thing. (01:10:32): I would tinker. I would build stuff. I would try and make the world around me more malleable. I just got an email this morning from someone who asked me about, "Oh, you think a lot about malleable software. Have you ever thought about what robotics might do?" And it just blew my mind because I had not, because it's so far from the skills that I have. But yeah, I don't know, something like that. Just I would do the same thing.
turns.zh: 实际上，我几乎会向我们招聘的每个人都提出这个问题。我自己也会做同样的事。我可能会花更少的时间开会和管理工作。我的工作中一个令人遗憾的地方是，我还没有用80%的自动化循环流程替代现有工作。真羡慕我们的工程师和设计师能做到这一点。希望未来我也能不用再做这份工作，但确实，我会做同样的事。（01:10:04）：我觉得我不编程是因为实用性，而是因为它也是一种智力挑战。所以我把它视为下棋和围棋。我很遗憾李世石输给AlphaGo或Zero后就放弃围棋了。我觉得没人在乎机器更擅长这件事，更重要的是人的智慧，继续努力就好。所以我也会做同样的事。（01:10:32）：我会鼓捣各种东西。我会创造东西，试图让周围的世界更具可塑性。今天早上我收到一封邮件，有人问我：“你对可塑性软件思考很多，有没有想过机器人技术能带来什么？”这让我很惊讶，因为这完全超出了我的专业领域。但确实，我不知道，或许会做类似的事。总之，我会继续做同样的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay. I'm going to take us to two recurring corners of the podcast to see what we find there. The first corner is contrarian corner. Is there something that you have a ... You have a lot of these already. I'm curious if there's anything else. (01:11:07): Is there something you have a contrarian opinion about, something you believe that a lot of people don't?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我要带大家去播客的两个常规环节，看看能发现什么。第一个环节是反常规观点。你有没有什么反常规的观点？你已经有很多这类观点了。我很好奇还有没有其他的。（01:11:07）：有没有什么你持反常规观点的事情？很多人的观点和你不同，你却坚信自己的看法？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: It's becoming so hard to have contrarian views because I think the algorithms just try and get contrarian views out of people with an insane force. Depending on the era, this may not be contrarian, but I think that inclusivity isn't always all that great. I think I very much believe in small group theory. I think the world is run by group chats of eight people or fewer. And so sometimes it's great to be exclusive. And what I mean by that is I even think about this in terms of Notion. (01:11:50): Notion could have the ambition to say, "We are going to have eight billion users." So every single person on the planet uses Notion. And I think if we did that, we would very much upset the first, call it, 500 million because the top of the class wants different things than everybody and everybody is in the top of the class at something. And so I think being okay with being exclusive sometimes is okay. (01:12:18): I will have to caveat this with, if you're McDonald's and you have exclusive hiring practices and it's the only job in a location, that is not what I'm talking about. But going back to comfy, air-conditioned job kind of thing is like, great, just work with and for the top of the class is sometimes a winning thing and just build a really, really good product for them, which by definition means you're going to exclude others.
turns.zh: 现在要持反常规观点越来越难了，因为我觉得算法会用疯狂的力量试图消灭反常规观点。不同时代有不同的反常规观点，但我认为包容性并不总是那么好。我非常相信小群体理论。我认为世界是由八人或更少人的群组聊天运行的。所以有时候排斥他人也没关系。我甚至用Notion来举例。（01:11:50）：Notion可能有野心说：“我们要拥有80亿用户。”让地球上每个人都用Notion。但如果我们真这么做了，会让现有的5亿用户很不爽，因为尖子生总是想要和别人不同的东西，而每个人在某些领域都是尖子生。所以有时候排斥他人也是可以的。（01:12:18）：我得补充一点，如果你是麦当劳，采用排他性招聘策略，而且当地只有这份工作，那就另当别论了。但回到舒适、空调房的工作环境这种事，就很棒了。和尖子生一起工作，为他们服务，有时就是赢家的策略。为他们打造一款真正优秀的产品，按定义来说就是要排斥其他人了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The TPPN guys have a really good way of describing this exact concept, which is they had like, I don't know, 8,000 listeners and a conversation. They got acquired for hundreds of millions of dollars, just like what's going on there? And the way they pitch it is, if we have millions of people listening to this thing, we've done something wrong. This is specifically designed for the people in power of tech to influence them, to teach them what's going on, and it worked out. It worked out great for them. So it's exactly what you're describing. (01:13:16): Okay, I'm going to take us now to fail corner. So people like you come on this podcast, they're like, "Okay, I'll get all these wonderful things." He's done and he's just killing it all the time. Everything's working. In reality, I'm sure not everything has worked in the course of your career. What's one example where things didn't work out and what did you learn from that experience?
turns.zh: TPPN 的团队在描述这个概念时做得很到位，他们举例说，比如他们当时有8000名听众和一次对话，结果被以数亿美元的价格收购。这里头到底怎么回事？他们的说法是，如果我们有数百万人在听我们的节目，那我们肯定做错了什么。这个产品是专门为科技行业的决策者设计的，目的是影响他们，教会他们行业动态，而这招确实奏效了。对他们来说，这正是你所描述的情形。（01:13:16）好的，现在我们来聊聊失败案例。像你这样的人来参加这个播客，人们会想：“好吧，我能得到所有这些美好的东西。”但现实中，你的职业生涯中肯定也遇到过不顺心的事。能分享一个失败的例子吗？从中你又学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Oh my God, it's such a weird ... I don't think about win versus fail. I feel like every day I fail a lot. What are big ones that annoy me? (01:13:46): Culturally, I think in running teams, I think a mistake that I made is at some point because hiring ... Now, it's easy, but at the time hiring designers that can code was quite challenging. And so then if you loosen that requirement, I did not predict how quickly that becomes like a slippery slope. And I would rather have had fewer designers that are more polymath. So I think that's one on organizational side. (01:14:14): On product, oh my God, I mean GitHub Actions and they're the ... I don't know, it's very technical, but the fact that we also thought we didn't need good package management for the actions. I don't know. I think the world would be better off if we had thought about that slightly harder. This is maybe like I started a competitor to Notion in 2014 and I didn't think of it as ... In fact, it wasn't a competitor of Notion because the week that we were going to get a term sheet from True Ventures, Notion pivoted from website building to document collaboration. And so True Ventures was like, "Hey, sorry, we have a conflict." And we're like, "Yep, no worries." (01:14:55): And we spent so much time polishing the editing experience. We did markdown folding, all the stuff that you now have in Obsidian, we did that back in 2014, and we thought that's the thing that really matters. And then Notion, by comparison, the first version of the Notion editor was terrible. It was all blocks. You couldn't even select between two blocks, but it turns out it didn't matter. And so I think that is just working diligently on the wrong thing for way too long, huge fail.
turns.zh: 天啊，这真是个奇怪的……我不去区分成功和失败。我觉得自己每天都在失败。哪些事让我特别烦心？（01:13:46）在团队管理方面，我觉得自己犯的一个错误是，在某个时候因为招聘……现在这挺容易的，但当时招聘能写代码的设计师还是很有挑战性的。所以如果你放宽这个要求，我没预料到这会迅速滑向歧途。我宁愿当时少招几个更全能的设计师。所以这在组织层面是个教训。（01:14:14）在产品方面，天啊，我说说GitHub Actions，他们……我也不知道，这太技术性了，但我们当时还以为不需要好的包管理系统。天啊，如果我们当时能更深入考虑一下这个问题就好了。比如我在2014年创办了一个Notion的竞争对手，但我没把它当作……事实上，它根本不是Notion的竞争对手，因为就在我们要从True Ventures拿到投资意向书的那一周，Notion就从网站搭建转向了文档协作。True Ventures当时就说，“嘿，不好意思，我们有冲突。”我们就说，“没关系，不用担心。” （01:14:55）我们花了大量时间优化编辑体验。我们做了Markdown折叠功能，所有这些你现在在Obsidian里能用到的功能，我们早在2014年就实现了，而且我们当时认为这才是关键所在。相比之下，Notion的首个编辑器版本糟透了。全是块状编辑器。你甚至无法在两个块之间进行选择，但结果证明这根本无关紧要。所以我觉得这就是在错误的方向上埋头苦干太久了，是个巨大的失败。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so interesting. Just coming back to your insight of when a product works, there's just this tiny core thing that is the thing that makes it amazing and what people want to come back to no matter how bad everything else is. I think that's a really interesting takeaway.
turns.zh: 这太有意思了。回到你对产品成功的见解，核心要素就是那个让产品令人惊叹、让人们无论其他方面多糟糕都愿意回来的东西。我觉得这真是很有启发的观点。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: We actually kept adding new features. At some point you go down to the death spiral, so we kept adding yet another feature of like, "Okay, is it good now? Is it good now?" And it's just, nope, the core wasn't good.
turns.zh: 我们实际上一直在添加新功能。到某个时候，你就会陷入死循环，所以我们不断添加新功能，心里还想：“好吧，现在好了吗？现在好了吗？” 但结果还是不行，核心部分根本没做好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's interesting. And in your experience, you can tell pretty quickly, "Okay. Wow. This has really taken off. We found something really powerful here."
turns.zh: 这很有意思。根据你的经验，你能很快判断出：“好吧哇，这个真的火了。我们在这里找到了非常强大的东西。”

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I think you can tell. Yeah, I think it's the obviously good thing. I think you're like, "Yep, this is good." And then it may be good in a way that you give it to users and every single user study that you do or whatever, just it falls flat and they don't know how to use it. (01:16:09): I think the important thing is actually to not give up on the core idea. And so that's 80%, but then the 20% is relentlessly iterate until it actually clicks with the folks that you're working for.
turns.zh: 我觉得你能看出来。我觉得这显然是个好主意。我觉得你会想，"没错，这很棒。"但有时候，即便你把它交给用户，进行用户研究或其他测试，结果却反响平平，用户根本不知道怎么用它。（01:16:09）：关键在于不要放弃核心理念。这占了80%，而剩下的20%就是要不断迭代，直到它真正能让用户心甘情愿地接受。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Max, is there anything else that you wanted to share with folks? Anything else you want to leave listeners with before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 马克斯，你还有什么想和大家分享的吗？在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你有什么想留给听众的吗？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: When I talk to young ... It's so funny to say that, but younger people in Silicon Valley. Right now, I think that Silicon Valley is uncharacteristically full of people who don't actually love computers. What I mean by that is it's like, "Oh, I want to make money." And of course everybody does. I like making money too. (01:16:54): I think there's this idea of this is the last train or what do we pose, the permanent underclass kind of stuff. And it is so detrimental to thinking about how you want to spend your heartbeats in life. And so I don't know, except ... The advice I would give is just don't let the rush or the frenzy distract you from the things that you actually care about and are passionate in life. I think it'll find a way. And that is not to mean that you shouldn't work hard. (01:17:28): I think you're actually way better off if you work incredibly hard from 18 to 25 or whatever. That's the way to go. You should work a lot and then later, you can work a little less. So it's more about the frenetic nature. You're so worried that if you don't win, if you don't take that last train out, you're going to be screwed. And it doesn't seem right to me. And I think it seems like a very hollow way of leading life. So I would encourage people to zoom out and not think about it that way. Read history, read computer science history maybe.
turns.zh: 当我和年轻人交流时……说起来挺有趣的，尤其是硅谷的年轻人。现在，我觉得硅谷异常充斥着那些不真正热爱计算机的人。我的意思是，他们总说：“哦，我想赚钱。”当然，人人都想赚钱。我也想赚钱。（01:16:54）：我觉得有种观念，认为这是最后一班车，或者说我们在假装什么，永远的底层阶级之类的。这对思考如何度过人生至关重要。我不知道该怎么说……我的建议就是别让浮躁和狂热分散你对真正热爱和充满激情之事的注意力。我觉得总会有办法的。但这并不意味着你不该努力工作。（01:17:28）：我觉得如果你在18到25岁之间拼命工作，那会好得多。这才是正确的道路。之后你可以稍微放松些。关键在于那种狂热的状态。你太担心如果不成功，如果错过最后一班车，就会完蛋了。在我看来这很不正常。我觉得这是一种空虚的人生观。所以我鼓励大家放宽眼界，别这样想。多读历史，或许多读计算机科学史。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's easy to hear that and feel like, "Okay, I'll be all right. I'm just going to work on things that I'm excited about." And then like, "Okay, but how will I actually have a job in the future?" I love the sentiment. Don't be so stressed about missing out on things and being in the permanent underclass. (01:18:17): Anything there that you think is important for people to do while not being overly stressed and worried about missing that train?
turns.zh: 听到这些，你可能会觉得，"好吧，我会没事的。我就去做让我兴奋的事吧。"然后又会想，"好吧，但未来我怎么才能找到工作呢？"我喜欢这种心态。别太焦虑，担心错过机会，别总觉得自己是永久的底层阶级。（01:18:17）：你觉得人们在不必承受太大压力、不用担心错过机会的情况下还能做些什么？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I don't know if it's Chris Rock, but there's a comedian that has this joke that is like, "It's great to follow your passion." And then he has this pause and is like, "If it pays." And so obviously, there is a little bit to that. I'm not suggesting that you don't worry about this at all. I think it's more that just tune down the amplitude of how much worry there is and then just realizing that history repeats itself more so than it is completely novel and new. (01:18:52): And then of course, yeah, if you tie it to agency and if you're not so stuck in, "Oh, I need certainty of how the world is going to unfold," you're probably going to be fine. And in the extreme, this is the other side of things, which is often if I then talk to people who are like, "Yep, but everything's going to change." I'm like, "Okay, great. So how is a move that you are going to make really going to shield you from it? And do you want to live in a society where all of this ..." I don't know, it just seems so insular, that mindset.
turns.zh: 我不知道是不是克里斯·洛克（Chris Rock），但有位喜剧演员讲过一个笑话，大意是"追随自己的热情很棒"。然后他停顿一下，接着说"前提是能赚到钱。"显然，这里面有两面性。我不是说你完全不必担忧，而是要降低担忧的强度，同时意识到历史往往会重演，而非完全创新。（01:18:52）当然，如果你能放下对未知的执着，不执着于"世界将如何发展"，你很可能就没问题了。极端情况下，另一种情况是，当我和那些说"是的，但一切都会改变"的人交谈时，我会问："好吧，那你打算采取的行动如何能真正保护你免受变化影响？你想生活在一个所有事情都被预先安排好的社会里吗？"我觉得这种心态太封闭了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With that, we have reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 接下来，我们将迎来激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有五个问题要问你们。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 你向他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: It depends on the person. I would say ... So Code by Charles Petzold, which is The Secret Language of Hardware and Software. It basically is like, "Do you know how computers actually work?" It is actually surprising to me how many professionally employed programmers don't know how computers work. That one, the funny thing is it does not have a line of code in it until chapter 27, so exceptionally good book. (01:20:05): I have a weird one, which is Tools of Conviviality by Ivan Illich. It's the contrast between, you look at the history of technology and tools that let users exercise human ingenuity and autonomy versus tools that are more at industrial scale that almost have become destructive to human autonomy. (01:20:31): And then the last one that I give mostly to executives that I think are creating a lot of systems is Seeing Like a State, which I think there is a famous stack overflow that popularized this, but it's the idea of, are you actually just designing a system so that you have legibility, but the way that you've created that legibility completely neglects the reality of the system on the ground. (01:21:00): And so I think of it as, great, you're the executive and you have these status reports and you think you know exactly how your teams work. If you actually spend time with the teams, you would realize that none of that is actually true. And so I think executives love creating fake legibility for themselves because we don't like noise as humans, right? We want the signal, but there's often less signal in it than one might think.
turns.zh: 这取决于对方。我会说……查尔斯·佩佐尔德（Charles Petzold）的《代码》（Code），即《硬件和软件的秘密语言》。这本书主要探讨“你知道计算机实际是如何工作的吗？”让我惊讶的是，许多专业程序员竟不了解计算机的工作原理。还有一本很有趣的书，伊凡·伊里奇（Ivan Illich）的《交往的工具》（Tools of Conviviality）。它对比了技术史上让用户发挥人类创造力和自主性的工具，以及更具工业规模、几乎对人类自主性造成破坏的工具。（01:20:05）最后一本我主要推荐给那些正在创建大量系统的管理者，那就是《像国家一样看》（Seeing Like a State）。我记得有个著名的 Stack Overflow 帖子让这本书广为人知，但其核心观点是，你设计一个系统时，可能为了可读性，但这种可读性却完全忽视了系统实际的运行环境。（01:21:00）所以我觉得，作为管理者，如果你有这些状态报告，认为自己完全了解团队运作情况，但如果你真正和团队共处，就会发现这些认知全是错觉。管理者之所以喜欢为自己创造虚假的可读性，是因为我们人类不喜欢噪音，对吧？我们想要信号，但信号往往比想象中更少。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Favorite recent movie or TV show that you have recently enjoyed?
turns.zh: 最近看过最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I have purposeful, terrible taste in movies, which is I want to watch movies that I never think about again after watching them. And I just want to be entertained and I mostly just want to see things that I couldn't remotely experience in real life. So you should not ask me for movie recommendations. (01:21:45): I did like Project Hail Mary a lot. I liked the book and I think the adaptation was really good. I think it also makes me super excited about any kind of future of humanity, which is I sometimes joke to our teams internally, which is like, okay, if we're really, really good at some point and Notion OS will be the thing that empowers five to eight people explore the galaxy somehow and everything will be organized for them in Notion. I don't know. I like this idea of pushing into space. (01:22:16): TV show, I'm late to this, The Handmaid's Tale. If you replace the concept of God with AI in that TV show, and then you don't actually have to squint that far to replace eyes with ICE in that TV show right now, it becomes a very, I don't know, the heavy show to watch in a good way.
turns.zh:
我的观影品味很特别，也很糟糕——我只想看那些看完就再也想不起来的。我只想找点乐子，看看那些现实生活中绝无可能经历的事。所以别来问我推荐电影了。（01:21:45）：我很喜欢《致命代码》这部电影。我读过原著，改编版也拍得很棒。它让我对人类的未来充满期待，有时我会跟团队开玩笑说，如果我们真能把 Notion OS 做到极致，五到八个人就能探索银河系，所有信息都能在 Notion 上井井有条地整理起来。我不知道，这种开拓太空的设想真的很酷。
（01:22:16）：说到剧集，我最近才追上《使女的故事》。如果把里面的上帝概念换成人工智能，再把眼睛换成 ICE（移民和海关执法局），也不算太牵强。现在看来，这部剧简直是反乌托邦的极致之作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I had not thought about that. Under His Eye, was that one of the things?
turns.zh: 哇，我之前从没这么想过。《上帝之眼》吗？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Yes. Under his AI.
turns.zh: 对，就是用人工智能替代上帝。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Whoa. No. Okay. I'm not afraid. I used to watch it and I'm more afraid to watch it now. Okay. Favorite product you've recently discovered that you really love. I know you put together a list of beautiful product that people buy. What's something recent?
turns.zh: 哇，不不不。好吧，我不害怕。我以前看过，现在再看反而更害怕了。好的，最近你发现的什么特别喜欢的产品？我知道你整理过一堆漂亮的产品清单。最近有没有新发现的？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Well, that list that I put together was for products that I think people should buy or that I thought ... I actually did the taste emulation. I'm like, "Oh, I think a lot of people are going to find this useful." I have weird ones now for you, which is ...
turns.zh: 嗯，我整理的那个清单是推荐人们应该买的产品，或者是我觉得……我其实做了品味模拟。我会说，“哦，我觉得很多人会觉得这个很有用。”现在我有些奇怪的推荐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: Okay. So it's a product. It's great. It's Ghostty Terminal Emulator. Most people use terrible terminals. Don't do that to yourself. Just use Ghostty. Huge fan of the work that Mitchell is doing. And then there is a new one for the phone called Moshi, M-O-S-H-I. That one's not free, but it looks very well done. I'm currently exploring it. I mostly code on the phone now because I don't have a real job. (01:23:47): There is an open source keyboard called ... I don't even know how to say it. Corne, C-O-R-N-E, which is a split keyboard. It looks very weird. The reason I like that one is I'm trying to claw back as much agency in my compute life as possible. This one is very open source. If you really wanted to, you could download all the schematics, send them off to China and you have the PCV back and you can just build it from scratch. (01:24:11): And then this one's silly, but I like tools. I like physical tools. CIVIVI pocket knife, which is pretty high quality, maybe more expensive than what most people would spend on a pocket knife. But I think a good pocket knife is a good tool to have.
turns.zh:
好的，是产品。很棒。Ghostty 终端模拟器。大多数人用的终端太烂了。别委屈自己了，用 Ghostty 吧。米切尔的工作太棒了。还有一个叫 Moshi 的手机应用，M-O-S-H-I。这款不免费，但做得很精良。我最近在研究它。现在我大部分时间都在手机上写代码，因为我没有正式工作。
（01:23:47）：有个开源键盘叫……我都不知道怎么说了。Corne，C-O-R-N-E，是分体式键盘。看起来很奇怪。我喜欢它的原因是我想尽可能多地夺回对计算生活的控制权。这款非常开源。如果你愿意，可以下载所有原理图，寄到中国，重新组装一台 PCV，从零开始搭建。
（01:24:11）：还有个挺傻的，但我喜欢实用的工具。CIVIVI 口袋刀，质量很高，也许比大多数人买口袋刀的预算贵。但我觉得一把好刀是个好工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: These are awesome. Very, very legit products. Okay. We'll link to them all. Two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you find yourself coming back to in work or in life?
turns.zh: 这些都很棒。非常靠谱的产品。好的，我们会把链接都放出来。最后两个问题。你有没有喜欢的座右铭，在工作或生活中经常回味的？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: It is very hard to remind yourself of that day-to-day, but I try to ... The universe has changed and life is what you make it. I think we love to cling to certainty and there is no certainty. (01:24:48): I could walk out of this room and could be the end of my life and live in the moment kind of thing. And life is what you make as sort of ... I think it's a Marcus Aurelius quote, I believe. And then, do you really want to know how it's going to end? No spoilers, just enjoy the ride.
turns.zh: 每天提醒自己这点真的很难，但我努力做到……宇宙已然变迁，生活由你自己创造。我想我们总爱执着于确定性，但世事本无定数。（01:24:48）：我可能走出这个房间，生命就此终结，所以活在当下才最重要。生活由你自己创造，这或许是马可·奥勒留的名言。那么，你真的想知道结局如何吗？不剧透了，就享受过程吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. You speak German. Do you have a favorite German word?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。你会说德语，有没有最喜欢的德语词？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
turns.en: I do. [foreign language 01:25:13], which is like tinker, but to me, it sounds like it has a less ... Tinker can sometimes be a little bit derogatory. And I think with the German equivalent, it's just not that harsh. And then the other one is [foreign language 01:25:32], which is the word for user, but it puts so much more emphasize on using up a thing. (01:25:40): As in, if you think about user, it's like you're using it, but using it up. And so then you think a lot more about the impermanence/the wastefulness of products that you might build if you use that word.
turns.zh: 有的。[外语 01:25:13]，意思是修补，但对我来说，它没那么贬义。德语里对应的词更温和。还有[外语 01:25:32]，意思是用户，但更强调耗尽某样东西。（01:25:40）：比如说用户，可能意味着你在使用它，但同时也在耗尽它。所以用这个词时，会让你更多地意识到产品易逝/浪费的本质，进而影响你设计产品时的决策。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. I love that you had quick answers to this question. Max, this was amazing. Thank you so much for doing this. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to ping you about anything? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你对这个问题的回答真快。马克斯，这次访谈太棒了。非常感谢你能来。最后两个问题。如果听众想联系你，哪里能找到你？他们如何能帮到你？

turns.speaker: Max Schoening
